2.5 Distribution Networks 63
Grounding the neutral through the Petersen coil is used for reducing the capaci-
tive current in isolated networks. The adequate inductance in the neutral is se-
lected for compensation of the capacitive current during a phase-to-ground fault;
thus this method is also known as the ground-fault compensation method. The
equivalent scheme for this arrangement is shown in Fig. 2.36. The coil reactance
is adjustable in relatively coarse steps, to allow for changes in network zero-
sequence capacitance resulting from the switching out of lines. If the coil induc-
tance exactly matches the system capacitance, the fault current has resistive char-
acter and may be insufficient for selective relay operation. Frequently, the ground-
ing equipment is completed with a resistor (resistor R in Fig. 2.36) that, with
g
some delay, automatically paralleling the coil what permits fault current sufficient
to correct relay operation.

An isolated network is one in which there is no intentional connection between
the circuit and ground (Fig. 2.37). The currents during single phase-to-ground
faults are low and depend mostly on the phase to ground capacitances of the lines.
The voltage between faulted equipment and ground is small, which improves
safety. However, transient and power-frequency overvoltages can be higher than
those obtained for other type of neutral grounding. Moreover, a one-phase ground-
ing results in the full line-to-line voltage appearing on the other two sound phases.
This situation can frequently cause failures in motors and transformers, due to in-
sulation breakdown. There are known difficulties in detecting and locating the
first line-to-ground fault: the overcurrent principle is not suitable here because the
capacitive current in a sound line may be even greater than that measured at the
faulted line [95, 97].

2.5.3 Network Representation
Distribution networks are different from transmission and sub-transmission sys-
tems in the following characteristics:
• they operate at lower voltages than transmission lines;
• they are usually used radially;
• they usually have tapped loads along the line, not just at the terminals (where
the measurements are available); and
• due to no line transposition and single-phase lateral and load, such networks
usually should be considered as unbalanced networks.
Usually we consider a distribution system as a three-phase main line with lat-
eral branches, some of which may be one- or two-phase circuits. Frequently, the
system is wye connected with a ground at the supply transformer and often with
multiple additional neutral grounds. The method of the neutral grounding has a
considerable influence on the value and character of the phase-to-ground fault cur-
rent. Practically, the impedance-based fault-location algorithms for phase-to-
ground faults can be used only in effectively grounding network. On the other
hand, the grounding method does not influence the accuracy for the other types of
faults (as for example phase-to-phase).

2.5 Distribution Networks 65
The above-mentioned remarks are particularly important for cable networks. In
branching points or laterals along the feeders, the cable sheaths are connected to-
gether and, generally, grounded through different resistances (Fig. 2.38a). Cable
sheaths usually remain connected even if the respective sections are disconnected
(Fig. 2.38b). This causes different equivalent schemes for positive/negative and
zero-sequence of the network.
The circuit model described earlier did not include the effects of frequency de-
pendence of the circuit parameters. Although this is unlikely to be a problem for
the overhead line sections, it is possible that some cable configurations may ex-
hibit a frequency dependence in the range 50–300 Hz, due to, for example, the
non-linearity of steel armor.

This could readily be incorporated into the circuit model using similar tech-

3 Power-line Faults – Models and Analysis
Abstract This chapter presents the basics of power-line faults. The fault models
are formulated using symmetrical-components and phase-coordinates approaches.
These models will be utilized in the fault-location algorithms presented in this
book. The analysis of arcing faults, including typical waveforms of current and
voltage signals, obtained from the ATP–EMTP simulation, is presented. Fault-
identification algorithms for fault detection, phase selection and directional dis-
crimination are briefly discussed.
3.1 Introduction
There are various causes of faults occurring in power systems. Breakdown of the
insulation can be caused by lightning strokes on overhead lines. As a result, the
connection with ground via a ground wire is established. Also, such ground con-
nection occurs when a tree or a man-made object provides the connecting path.
Some faults are also caused by switching mistakes of the station personnel.
Power-system faults can be shunt, series or a combination of shunt and series
faults. Under a shunt fault there is a flow of current between two or more phases,
or between phase(s) and ground. A series fault is an abnormality at which the im-
pedances of the three phases are not equal, usually caused by the interruption of
one or two phases.
Most of the power-system faults occur in transmission networks, especially on
overhead lines. Lines are the elements in the system that are in charge of trans-
porting important bulks of energy from generator plants to load centers. Due to
their inherent characteristic of being exposed to atmospheric conditions, transmis-
sion lines have the highest fault rate in the system. Therefore, a number of re-
searchers have devoted great effort to the line protection and fault location.
There are various known fault statistics, which are related to different voltage
levels, technical and weather conditions. All of them unambiguously indicate that
around 75% of the total number of power-system faults occurs in transmission
networks. This fact reveals the very high importance of fault analysis for transmis-
sion networks.

68 3 Power-line Faults – Models and Analysis
3.2 Fault on Power Lines
Faults on EHV/UHV overhead lines are in majority single-phase-to-ground arcing
faults and are mostly temporary. Therefore, protective relays are provided with the
automatic reclosing function [8, 53, 300]. This function allows the line to be re-
closed and kept in operation after the fault has disappeared because the arc can
self-extinguish. The circuit breakers can operate on a single phase (single pole) or
on all three phases. For applying a proper autoreclosing option the fault type is re-
quired to be correctly recognized by the fault-location techniques [55, 171, 177].
The main characteristic of faults is related to the fault impedance involved,
which can basically be considered as fault resistance. In this respect, the faults are
categorized as bold and resistive ones, respectively. Usually, for inter-phase faults,
fault resistances are small and in general do not exceed 0.5 Ω. They may, how-
ever, become much higher during ground faults, because tower footing resistance
may be as high as 10 Ω [174]. If there is a flashover of an insulator, the connec-
tion of towers with ground wires makes the resulting fault resistance smaller. In
practice, it seldom exceeds 3 Ω. For some ground faults the fault resistances may
become much higher, which happens in cases of fallen trees, or if a broken con-
ductor lies on the high-resistive soil [326].
3.2.1 Fault Types
For formulating fault-location algorithms mostly the basic linear models of faults,
such as presented in Fig. 3.1, are considered. The fault resistance involved is de-
noted by R and the resistance connected to ground in the case of inter-phase faults
F
involving ground (Figs. 3.1c and e) by R. Note that it is assumed that the fault resis-
g
tance R for inter-phase faults (Figs. 3.1b–e) is identical in all phases. Such basic fault
F
models are considered for both the symmetrical components approach and the phase
co-ordinates approach as well.
Besides numerous fault-location techniques considering the basic linear fault
models, there have also been developed some algorithms considering the electric-
arc phenomenon [51, 54, 190, 191, 244]. Also, this phenomenon is widely used in
digital simulations [169, 170, 217] aimed at evaluating the performance of the al-
gorithms based on the linear fault models.
Broken-conductor or open-conductor failure in one phase (phase a) is shown in
Fig. 3.2a. However, such a failure may also happen in two phases. Broken-
conductor failure may also occur coupled with this phase-to-ground fault (Figs.
3.2b and c). For such combined faults, different sequences, as seen from the mea-
suring point (M in Figs. 3.2b and c) can be considered. For a fault from Fig. 3.2b,
an open-conductor failure is located outside the fault loop seen from the measur-
ing point, while it is inside for the case of Fig. 3.2c. Such two combined faults
(Figs. 3.2b and c) impose different conditions on fault location [110].

Sometimes more than one fault can occur simultaneously. For example, these
may all be shunt faults, as shown in Fig. 3.3, where a phase-to-ground fault occurs
in combination with a phase-to-phase fault for the remaining phases. In general,
different fault resistances (R , R ) can be involved in these faults.
F1 F2
Double faults [238] are considered as faults to ground, occurring simultane-
ously at two different locations in one or several circuits. In Fig. 3.4a, such a fault,
also called a cross-country fault is shown as occurring on a double-circuit line.
Flashover faults on a double-circuit line (Fig. 3.4b) are usually caused by a
lightning stroke to ground wire or tower, or due to a direct lightning stroke to a
phase conductor [39].

A fault involving two different nominal power-system voltages is called an in-
ter-system fault. Such faults can occur on transmission lines hung on the same
tower and rated at different voltages.
Besides the faults described, there are also multiple faults, as for example,
faults to ground occurring simultaneously at more than two different locations in
one or several circuits originated from a common source.

3.2.2 Fault Statistics
Numerous statistics data concerning power-system faults are available in the lit-
erature and Internet. They differ depending on which power-system element is
considered and on the voltage level. In order to be acquainted briefly with the fault
statistics for power transmission lines, in Tables 3.1 and 3.2 the representative da-
ta [109] is provided. In general, the number of faults decreases with an increase of
the voltage level (Table 3.1). As regards the fault type, it is the single phase-to-
ground faults that most frequently occur (Table 3.2).

3.2.3 Models of Resistive Faults in Symmetrical Components
There is a wide group of fault-location algorithms that require determining the to-
tal fault current (I F ), i.e., the current flowing through the fault-path resistance.
These are mainly fault-location algorithms utilizing one-end measurement. Also,
the majority of two-end or multi-end fault-location algorithms, but not utilizing
complete three-phase voltage and current measurements, belong to this group. Use
of complete measurements of three-phase voltage and current at both ends, or at
all ends in the case of multi-terminal lines, allows determination of the total fault
current to be avoided.

72      3 Power-line Faults – Models and Analysis
In general, since the total fault current (I ) is an immeasurable quantity, it can
F
be calculated [115, 124] or estimated [62, 109, 121] by expressing it with the
measured quantities, the network parameters and the unknown distance to fault. If
the currents from all line terminals are available, then the total fault current can be
calculated. However, since the required total fault current is calculated with use of
the distant measurements, a special calculation method aimed at minimizing the
influence of the line shunt capacitances charging has to be applied [124]. When
the currents from all line terminals are not available, then the total fault current
has to be estimated.
However, for both the above-mentioned cases (calculation or estimation of the
total fault current) the total fault current can be expressed as the following
weighted sum of its symmetrical components:

Analogously, determination of the total fault current can be considered for the
other fault types.
Different priority with respect to using the particular symmetrical components
[62, 109, 121] can be applied, as for example:
• use of the zero-sequence is generally avoided since the zero-sequence imped-
ance for the overhead line is considered as an uncertain parameter;
• use of the negative- instead of positive-sequence is preferred, because the line
shunt capacitance charging is more extensive for the positive-sequence;
• use of both positive- and negative-sequence, excluding the zero-sequence
(I =1.5I +1.5I for the fault considered in the above example) is preferred,
F F1 F2
as it allows the calculations to be made simpler [62, 122].
Instead of using the positive-sequence components, which for three-phase bal-
anced faults are present alone, the incremental (superimposed) positive-sequence
components are recommended due to a reduced shunt capacitance effect [3–5,
225].

3.2.4 Models of Resistive Faults in Phase Coordinates
If a line considered is untransposed or if there are devices switched into the line
that during faults introduce additional asymmetry, a description of the faulted
network can be performed using the phase-coordinates approach [135, 136, 216,
274]. Series capacitors equipped with metal-oxide varistors are such devices [86,
111, 274] introducing the phase asymmetry.
A generalized fault model [109, 272, 284, 285] is presented in Fig. 3.5. It al-

• normally open switch, if there is no such connection.

3.2 Fault on Power Lines 81
3.2.5 Arcing Faults
According to the fault current state, the fault arc [134, 170, 300] is classified as:
• primary arc; and
• secondary arc.
The primary arc occurs during flashover of the line insulator string, caused by
lightning stroke or other reasons. The secondary arc follows the primary one
when the faulted phase circuit breaker trips, as is sustained by mutual coupling be-
tween the healthy and faulted phases.
The primary arc appears after fault inception and lasts until single-phase trip-
ping of the faulted phase. It shows generally a deterministic behavior as observed
in the field and laboratory arc tests [314]. After isolating the fault (by single-phase
tripping) there is a secondary arc, which is sustained by the capacitive and induc-
tive coupling to the sound phases. The secondary arc usually self-extinguishes.
The secondary arc has extremely random characteristics affected by the external
conditions around the arc channel.
A vast majority of fault-location algorithms process current and voltage signals
from the fault interval (starting from the fault inception until the circuit-breaker
operation) and in some cases of the pre-fault interval (just before the fault incep-
tion). For these algorithms the primary arc is of interest. However, it mainly con-
cerns simulations performed for evaluating the fault-location algorithms under
study. This is so since the vast majority of fault-location algorithms apply a linear
model of the fault path for their formulation. Only a few fault-location algorithms
take into account the primary-arc model.
In [304], it is shown that by measuring voltage on the line side of a circuit
breaker, the location of a permanent fault can be calculated using the transient
caused by the fault-clearing operation of the circuit breaker. Due to the fault-
clearing operation of the circuit breaker, a surge is initiated and travels between
the opened circuit breaker and the fault, if the latter is still present. The distance to
fault is determined by measuring the propagation time of the surge from the
opened circuit breaker to the fault. In this relation, modeling the secondary arc is
important.

hysteresis. Extensive studies in [134, 170, 300] have shown that the dynamic volt-

3.3 Fault-identification Algorithms
Fault identification is the first task in the fault-location algorithm. It includes fault
detection, type of fault and direction determination that are needed for correct
fault-loop determination. Generally, the used algorithms are similar to that applied
for protective relaying purposes, however, as realized off-line, may adopt more
sophisticated principles for error reducing. Frequently, that part of the common
procedure is realized by the protective relay that delivers to the fault locator re-
quired information on the identified fault and the recorded data.
3.3.1 Fault Detection
A number of approaches to fault detection are proposed in the literature. The ab-
normal conditions (not necessarily faults) are detected by watching the phase im-
pedances and/or phase-current amplitudes and/or phase-voltage amplitudes and/or
zero-sequence current amplitude. Depending on a particular application, different
activation criteria are combined in a different way. To speed up the fault detection,

88 3 Power-line Faults – Models and Analysis
one may also apply derivatives of the relevant signals. It is quite easy to introduce
adaptivity to such approaches. Knowing the breaker positions, monitoring the av-
erage load of a line, etc., the thresholds may be self-adjusted to improve the sensi-
tivity and reliability of fault detection [148].
The general structure of the fault-detection algorithm is presented in Fig. 3.11.
The used criteria are based on a statistical approach. Two different statistical
measures of the voltage or current signal are determined in parallel filters F1 and
F2 and some criterion value is formulated to assess the fault inception. Below, we
present more useable realizations.
Filter F1
x(k) d(k)

Filter F2
Fig. 3.11 General structure of fault-detection algorithm
Much easier methods refer directly to samples of current and/or voltage wave-
forms (Fig. 3.12). Disregarding a particular solution, two approaches are consid-
ered [77]:
• A sample-by-sample method computing numerically the first derivative of a
watched signal. If this derivative overruns a pre-set value, an auxiliary counter
starts to count up. This counter is incremented by the absolute value of the de-
rivative. When it reaches another pre-set threshold, a fault is confirmed. Cer-
tainly, the first threshold must be set above the maximum value of the scaled
derivative under normal conditions.
• A cycle-by-cycle algorithm compares a present sample with the sample one cy-
cle back. The threshold for such a difference may be set much lower than in the
sample-by-sample method. An auxiliary counter may be used to initiate when
the absolute value of the defined difference overruns its threshold [77]. The
fault is detected when the counter increased by the successive differences over-
reaches the second threshold.
Another method relies on the absolute difference between the MEAN and
MEDIAN filters outputs [77]:

The algorithm detects high-impedance faults on an overhead line based upon the

NERM measures.

If the defined measures (3.13)–(3.15) overreach their pre-defined threshold a
fault is being confirmed.
The observed signals in the case of series-compensated lines are affected by the
series capacitors and their MOVs transients. During faults MOVs switch between
linear and non-linear modes generating a variety of harmonics in the signals. Un-
der high-resistance faults sub-synchronous oscillations may occur also. The per-
formed study of series-compensated line transients proved that the measures
(3.13)–(3.15) can be successfully adopted for fault detection in such lines [146].
Moreover, such fault detectors can be designed for detecting a certain class of
faults. Namely, it is of vital importance to provide the decision whether or not the
series capacitor (-s) is involved in a fault loop.
When considering a fault-detection issue it is worth listing traveling-wave ap-
proaches too. Correct classification of all types of faults from the information
available at the local bus appears difficult, therefore a communication channel is
required. However, significant improvement has been made by utilizing some ex-
tra information present at the local bus and related to the subsequent wave reflec-
tions [20, 40].
There are also several applications of artificial neural networks (ANNs) to fault
detection. The most typical is aimed towards arcing fault detection [171]. Such al-
gorithms are usually combined with other fault-identification purposes [239].
Some of them are considered in Chap. 9.
3.3.2 Phase Selection
Again, changing of different electrical values during fault are utilized for type of
fault determination. The simplest method assumes that a phase impedance (result-
ing from a phase voltage and current) for a phase involved in a fault is below a
certain level – correlated with the maximum load. In addition, the zero-sequence
quantities (current and/or voltage) are used as indicators of faults with the ground.
Instead of processing voltage and current samples directly, superimposed current
and voltage samples can be used for fault classification too [12, 17].
Another family of methods uses relationships between the symmetrical compo-
nents of the fault current and/or voltage. For speeding up of detection and to ob-
tain more reliable decision, information about phase angle is used [148]. Two fault
signatures: negative-sequence vs. positive-sequence and negative-sequence vs.
zero-sequence current and/or voltage are used simultaneously. The criterion is
based on checking the relations between adequate post-fault angles, which change

3.3 Fault-identification Algorithms      91
significantly faster just after fault than do magnitudes. Let us present this method
in more detail.
Generally, the approach based on using symmetrical components introduces the
following three criteria spaces [148]:
•  negative-sequence versus positive-sequence relation;
•  negative-sequence versus zero-sequence relation; and
•  significant increase of the positive-sequence quantity with absence of the nega-
tive- and zero-sequence components.
Using these criteria spaces it is possible to identify different types of fault. De-
tailed criteria can be defined with respect to different features of the considered
sequence components. The second condition was added because it is well known
that the presence of large negative-sequence components in the relay input signals
reveals the occurrence of a fault in the supervised system. This is so for all faults
but excluding the case of the balanced three-phase fault, for which only the posi-
tive-sequence current is present, however, with the increased value after a fault
occurrence.
Unfortunately, during faults there are transients in the measured currents and
thus the symmetrical components are determined with certain errors. Moreover,
accuracy and speed of operation are in opposition, so the developer should decide
on some kind of compromise.
Symmetrical components are defined for phasors of a three-phase system.
There are known correct methods that are based on the full-cycle Fourier algo-
rithms [193, 237], state observers [257] or Kalman filters [82]. In fast procedures
the current phasors should be calculated with use of an adequately simple method.
Such a method is proposed below.

3.3.3 Directional Detection
A directional element becomes essential for a complete distance relay when a fault
to be cleared occurs very close to a relaying point. In the fault locators such a tool
may be important when both lines (forward and backward) have different charac-
teristics, e.g., one of them is series-compensated. The traditional approach to miti-
gate the problem of the voltage fall in distance relays is to apply an additional po-
larization voltage. It may be done by [287]:
• cross-polarization of a voltage signal; and
• memory polarization of a voltage signal.
In the fault locators information on direction to fault is immediately used for
distance to fault estimation.
The traditional concept is based on computing the increments in positive-
sequence voltage and current (by subtracting the pre-fault positive sequence quan-
tities from the post-fault ones) [209]. The pre-fault values are recommended to be
understood as delayed by 5 cycles. The impedance resulting from the increments
of positive-sequence current and voltage is calculated as follows:
U −Upre
∆Z = 1 1 (3.23)
1 I −Ipre
1 1
where Upre, U are positive-sequence voltages for pre- and fault periods, and
1 1
analogously for currents.
Relation (3.23) enables very reliable direction detection. For a forward fault
such an impedance is a local source impedance (as to the value and with the nega-
tive sign to account for the fact that the current is flowing from a source to a for-
ward fault location). While for a reverse fault, this impedance equals the line im-
pedance plus the remote source impedance. Certainly, for a series-compensated
line, the line impedance must be understood as the line inductive impedance itself
plus the capacitive impedance of the series RC equivalent of the parallel arrange-
ment of a series capacitor and its MOV.
Figure 3.15 presents the performance of the positive-sequence directional ele-
ment under a sample forward fault close to the substation (Fig. 3.15a) and reverse
fault (Fig. 3.15b) in a 400-kV system. In the first case (forward fault) the imped-
ance (3.23) establishing the steady-state position in the third quadrant of the com-
plex plane Its value is equal to the local system source impedance multiplied by
(–1). For the backward fault the impedance resulting from the increments of posi-
tive-sequence voltage and current locates in the 1st quadrant and settles at the
value equal to the line impedance plus the remote source impedance.

4 Signal Processing for Fault Location
Abstract This chapter presents the basic signal-processing methods applied in the
fault location for measurement of the electrical quantities and formulation the es-
timation procedures. This methods can be divided into three categories depending
on signals representation and analytical tools used: frequency domain, time do-
main and time-frequency representation methods. All the three methods are dis-
cussed in this chapter from the point of view of their application to the fault-
location algorithms.
4.1 Introduction
The estimate of distance to fault in a line is a function of network model parame-
ters and measurements. This chapter gives a general review of the methods used
for measuring the adequate quantities for fault location. Representation of the
measured variables depends on the assumed network model. From that point of
view one can distinguish the following methods for description of the state of an
analyzed network:
• Specification of the relation between currents and voltages by means of time-
domain functions. This representation is closely related to the classical circuit
theory where transients phenomena are described in a form of a set of algebraic
(copying Kirchhoff’s laws) and differential equations (imitating a circuit-
elements models). In the discrete-time domain differential equations are substi-
tuted by adequate difference relations. Such an approach is suitable for appro-
priate representation of a circuit dynamics [30, 50].
• The circuit description under assumption that the observed process is stable. In
an AC system that is equivalent to the foundation that all the process variables
(voltages and currents) are sinusoidal with constant magnitude and angle veloc-
ity ω. In such a condition a network may be entirely defined by use of voltage
and current phasors and impedance (admittance) for the network parameters
representation that is originated from the Fourier-transform (FT). Unlike in
previous approaches, principally the time is not directly represented in phasors:
all process variables are stationary. Such a treatment is also called frequency-
domain circuit analysis [50, 84].

98 4 Signal Processing for Fault Location
• Representation of an observed process as a dynamic one (as in the first men-
tioned approach) but with utilization of some of the tools and results obtained
from the frequency-domain analysis. Such an approach arose from a desire to
apply frequency-domain tools to analysis of a non-stationary process. This
method is called the multi-resolution analysis and is connected with application
of tools like the short time Fourier transform (STFT), the wavelet transform
(WT) and others [167, 246, 249].
Parameters of the considered network (fault-loop parameters in the fault-
location procedures) are determined by using the network model and measure-
ments. As the network model is considered one can distinguish lumped- and dis-
tributed-parameters models. In this book we consider digital measurements, which
is connected with conversion of continuous-time voltages and currents to their dis-
crete representation at the input to the measurement unit.
Since the vast majority of digital protective relays and other controlling devices
(including fault locators) is still based on phasors, the issue of phasor estimation is
probably the single most investigated and documented subject in research on digi-
tal relaying and fault location [250]. Irrespective of the chosen circuit representa-
tion the voltage and current phasor estimation is inherently connected with a sig-
nal processing applied in fault location. Therefore, this chapter is mainly
concentrated on the phasor-estimation problem.
4.2 Time-Versus Frequency-domain Analysis
The fault locator acquires information on the supervised process (connected with a
fault on the line) through analog-to-digital converters (ADC) in a form of recorded
voltages and currents samples. Naturally, the sampling proceeds in time convert-
ing this independent variable from continuous to discrete form. Observed voltage
or current waveforms that vary over time (time-domain function) may be consid-
ered as examples of the more general concept of the signal. Consequently, the
voltage or current measured at the output of instrument transformers represents the
continuous-time signal, while the recorded samples correspond with the discrete-
time signal.
A continuous-time circuit may be analyzed by using the classical circuit theory
where dynamical relations are represented by differential equations. For example,
for a lumped-parameters circuit as in Fig. 4.1a one can write as follows:

A Laplace transform (e.g., U(s)) may be considered as a function in the fre-

Replacing the circuit equations in the form of differential equations as in (4.1)
by adequate Laplace-domain equations – as in (4.6) – considerably simplifies an
analysis of the circuit dynamics (differential equations are reduced to algebraic
equations). Therefore, the Laplace transform plays an important role in analysis of
such systems. It is the cornerstone of classical circuits, systems and control theory.
A direct relation between time and frequency domains is defined by the Fourier
transform, which, as was shown, is immediately connected with the Laplace trans-
form. The classical Fourier transform is defined by the following pair of integrals:

In the digital measurement systems considered here the continuous-time func-

There is a known relation between the continuous and discrete-time domain of
the signal. It is defined by the sampling theorem (known also as the Shannon sam-
pling theorem or the Nyquist sampling theorem). The sampling theorem indicates
that a continuous-time signal can be unambiguously represented in a discrete form
only if it does not contain frequency components above one-half of the sampling
rate [230]. Under such conditions the samples are a unique representation of the
signal. The proper sampling (with respect to the sampling theorem) enables the
exact reconstruction of the analog signal from the samples.
The Laplace transform applied for discrete-time signals and functions leads to a
Z-transform, where for convenience, the operator s is adequately replaced by an
operator z [30, 50]:

4.2 Time-Versus Frequency-domain Analysis 103
In digital signal processing the index k is counted from 0 that reduces (4.18) to a
so-called unilateral Z-transform.
The Z-transform is a powerful tool for analysis of discrete-time systems. Simi-
larly to the Laplace transform, it can be used to solve linear constant-coefficient
difference equations. In other words, instead of solving these equations directly,
we transform them into a set of algebraic equations first, and then solve in this
transformed domain. Therefore, we can consider the Z-transform as a discrete-
time counterpart of the Laplace transform.
It is a well-known consequence of the continuous-time signal sampling in the
frequency domain: discrete-time signals have a periodic frequency spectrum and
the period depends on sampling frequency [230]. For illustration of this principle
let us consider an exponential continuous-time signal of the form (Fig. 4.2a):

FIR filters may be easily designed with linear phase characteristic and therefore

The algorithms designed for power-system automation and control purposes
should meet two contradictory demands:
• results of measurement (estimation) should be available as soon as possible;
and
• measurement accuracy should satisfy expectations related to the sensitivity and
selectivity of the final decision made by the controlling device.
In the case of fault-location procedures the requirements for the ratio of veloc-
ity action are somewhat less but, on the other hand, expectations regarding the ac-
curacy increase. The important circumstances that need to be taken into considera-
tion when designing the measurement algorithms are the fact that the observed
system was corrupted during a fault. This causes a sudden dynamical process that
changes the measurement condition and that is exactly the most interesting mo-
ment from the control devices point of view. But in transient conditions the ob-
served process (represented by a signal) has too many unknown parameters that
need to be identified for describing it. The usual way is to simplify the considered
process model leaving only those characteristics that are important for the given
task. In the next section, the development of this approach is described that has led
to the methods used contemporarily.

4.3 Phasor-based Algorithms      109
4.3 Phasor-based Algorithms

riodical excitation the response is tracking the input signal with the same fre-
quency. For mathematical convenience in finding the output, we let the input

In the considered linear system the real and imaginary parts of the output corre-
spond to the real and imaginary parts of the complex forcing signal. Practically,
we want the response to the real part (the cosine) so we simply take the real part of
the output as the result.
The application of the phasor concept to the solution of AC circuit steady-state
problems was proposed by Ch. Steinmetz4 and was first presented to an astonished
audience at the International Electrical Congress in 1893 [302]. The main simpli-
fication of the method consists in transformation of the set of differential equa-
tions that described a linear electric circuit into a set of complex algebraic equa-
tions. The input–output relations are reduced to multiplication of the input phasor
by the transfer function (which may have the form of an impedance, an admittance
or another parameters) represented by a complex number. In fact, the transforma-
tion between the time domain and the frequency domain is applied here (regarding
a signal and a network parameter) but thanks to an introduced simplification the
concept delivers effective tool for AC circuits analysis and measurements.
Besides the network calculations the phasor transformation also plays an im-
portant role in the measurements and the circuit-parameters identification. In a
computer-based control system in both the aforesaid applications we need to esti-
mate the voltage and current phasors from sampled instantaneous waveforms.
Note that the phasor concept meets the pre-supposed demand concerning the sim-
plification of the signal model: transients are neglected and only one harmonic
4 Charles Proteus Steinmetz (1865–1923), born Carl August Rudolph Steinmetz in Breslau,
Germany (now Wroclaw, Poland).

4.3 Phasor-based Algorithms 111
component is considered. The next section presents the voltage- and current-
phasors estimation algorithms.
4.3.1 Phasor Measurement
Since the vast majority of computer-based power-system control devices is still
based on phasors, the issue of phasor estimation is probably the single most inves-
tigated and documented subject in research on power-system relaying and control.
The digital phasor estimators are designed to meet several contradictory require-
ments, namely: to be fast, immune to frequency excursions, and insensitive to sig-
nal pollution including harmonics, sub-harmonics, high-frequency oscillations,
noise and decaying DC components [137, 237, 249].
Basic fault-location algorithms are derived on an assumption that the post-fault
state can be considered as a steady-state one. Consequently, in an AC system
fault-loop voltage and current can be represented in the form of sinusoidal wave-
forms. These waveforms may be expressed in the frequency domain as phasors.
We can see that the phasor in (4.30) has the same form as the exponential repre-
sentation of the signal spectrum (4.12) and both representations will be the same
for ω=ω.
1
Below, we present the basic methods for determination of voltage and current
phasors from instantaneous sampled waveforms (signals). They are closely related
to the general Fourier transform so we start from a presentation of a family of the
Fourier methods suitable for digital signal processing.
We have seen in the previous section that the detailed rule of the Fourier trans-
form depends on the type of considered signals. From the practical point of view
the following types of signals are important [230, 298]:
• A continuous-time signal x(t) for which the general Fourier transform (4.10),
(4.11) is applied (if the signal fulfils the Fourier integral convergence).
• A continuous-time signal x(t) is periodic with a period T; such a signal can be
represented as the complex Fourier series and its coefficients can be interpreted
as the spectral representation of x(t).
• A discrete-time signal x#(k) is obtained from sampling a signal x(t) with sam-
pling period T. The pair of the Fourier transform is as follows:

and is known as the discrete Fourier transform (DFT).
Practically important is the last case defining the DFT representation. It is the
basic method used in digital signal processing. In practical application a discrete
signal is limited to M samples (even if it is longer) assuming zeros outside this in-
terval. Results of the direct transformation (4.37) are samples of the Fourier series
coefficients X(n) that define the discrete periodic spectrum of series x(k). It can be
seen that X(n)=X(n+rM), r – an integer number, but we are interested in values of
X(n) only in the interval 0≤n≤M–1 because they have important physical interpre-
tation: considering the signal x(k) has the period on N, then X(n)= X (n)+j X(n)
R I
can be interpreted as the complex magnitude of the nth harmonic, n=0, 1, .., M–1.
Similarly, the signal x(k) is either a finite-length sequence of length M, or it is a
periodic sequence with period M.

Substituting in (4.49) the cosine and sine functions from (4.48) we can check
that the orthogonality condition is satisfied if the data window length is a multiple
of half the period of the correlation function: M=mN/2, m – natural value.
It would be interesting to compare both the presented methods defined by
(4.47) and (4.48). Some results are shown in Fig. 4.9. The input signal is the same
as in Fig. 4.7. Application of the algorithm (4.47) gives results as in Fig. 4.9a (the
phasor components) and Fig. 4.9b – changing of the phasor phase, while Figs 4.9c
and d present results obtained from the algorithm (4.48). Note that in both cases
the data window is filling up to k= 15 (the algorithm transient period). The phasor
components of the first algorithm form a sinusoidal waveform with the same fre-
quency as the correlation functions. At the steady state the phase increases at each
step by the angle ν. The results of the algorithm (4.48) form the constant compo-
nents (the observed small variations result from the signal transients). It is not sur-
prising that both algorithms give the same magnitude of the estimated phasors.

The similar forms can also be defined for other types of the algorithms. We
should remember, however, that the recursive form (4.51) is hazardous when the
algorithm is continuously realized in a floating-point processor due to possible er-
rors accumulating in successive steps.
Stable output for using the presented full-period Fourier algorithms is available
only after one period from the beginning of the processing. Such a long delay may
not be acceptable if the operation action is faster or if an after-fault stage is shorter
than one period. In such a case we can use the half-period Fourier algorithm. Simi-
larly to (4.47) we can write:

of the considered algorithms.

From the provided analysis we can see that the phasors for both orthogonal

Least Squares Method Application
The general problem in designing the signal-parameters estimator is to choose an
appropriate model for the signal representation and to define a procedure for the
model-parameters estimation. In the methods proposed above the model was for-
mulated in the form of an adequately defined correlation function (DFT) or im-
pulse function of the FIR filter. In the following part of this section we present the
tool for estimators that uses the least squares method (LSM).
In the digital signal processing the LSM technique applies to problems where
data are given from measurements with associated uncertainties that influence the
fit made to them. The LSM criterion specifies that the sum of squared differences
between the postulated signal model and its estimates are minimal.5 For a two-
state model (4.61) successive measurements can be arranged in the form [137,
249]:

4.3.2 DC Component Consideration
While voltage signals are practically not contaminated with decaying DC compo-
nents, currents can contain exponentially decaying DC offsets with unpredictable
initial magnitude and unknown time constant. This is so due to both the fault resis-
tance and the fault incipience angle being random factors. The decaying DC offset
in a fault current can result in nearly twenty per cent overshoot in the estimated
magnitude depending on the used algorithm [307]. This has to be taken into ac-
count when setting fast digital relays. In fault location a DC component influences
the distance to fault estimation error, especially when the fault record is relatively
short.
Generally, the phasor estimators can be easily designed to remove a pre-defined
DC component [237, 258, 306]. The problem arises, however, when the time con-
stant of the DC offset is not known. Several approaches have been put forward so
far to minimize the influence of a decaying DC component on phasor estimation.
The most practical solution merges a digital mimic filter with any robust phasor
estimator such as the full-period Fourier algorithm. The digital mimic filter repro-
duces numerically an analog mimic circuit commonly applied in traditional line

130 4 Signal Processing for Fault Location
protection [137, 237]. The original mimic circuit is a differentiating element, and
therefore, its digital replica is a high-pass digital filter [18, 237]. This, in turn, re-
sults in a worsened frequency characteristic of the resulting phasor estimator. The
strong asset of a digital mimic filter is its significant robustness to the actual (ran-
dom) value of the time constant.
The other approach is to include an exponentially decaying DC component into
the signal model and apply certain curve-fitting techniques to design a phasor es-
timator. Usually, the DC offset is dealt with as a noise, represented by either de-
terministic or probabilistic characteristics, rather than a parameter to be fitted [18,
237]. Several specific estimators originate from this general approach:
• Linear estimators when applied to suppress a DC component deal with the non-
linear exponential function by using the first few terms of its Taylor series
[258].
• The least squares method (LSM) yields non-recursive or recursive estimators
[108, 137, 262]. The latter can be modified by introducing resetting or forget-
ting factors for better absorption of non-harmonic frequencies including the de-
caying DC component.
• Application of a state-variable model brings forth estimators in the form of a
state observer [257] or a Kalman filter [78]. The requirement for rarely avail-
able a priori noise characteristics is, however, the key disadvantage of the latter
measuring technique.
Yet another, numerically simpler, approach to a decaying DC component is to
apply a cosine filter for estimating both the direct (cosine filter) and quadrature
(cosine filter delayed by one-fourth of a cycle) orthogonal components [307]. Ad-
ditional delay slowing down the estimator's response is, though, the main disad-
vantage of this approach.
The aforementioned methods, although they improve the measurement, do not
reject a DC component perfectly. Below, we present yet another algorithm that
fully rejects a DC component from the input signal regardless of its time constant
and the initial magnitude.

Following the above description of the algorithm we can prepare the MATLAB
procedure as follows (function dc_lsm.m).
function [Xc,Xs,XR,XI,del_c,del_s]=dc_lsm(N,f1,x_k);
% inputs: N – number of samples per cycle
% f1 – system frequency
% x_k – recorded input signal
%outputs: Xc, Xs – components of corrected phasor
% XR, XI – components of the phasor (Fourier alg.)
% del_c, del_s – introduced corrected signals
a=2*pi/N;
t1=1/f1; % system frequency period
tamx=0.3; % max. decaying time const.
tamn=0.004; % min. decaying time const.
rsmx=exp(-t1/(N*tamx));
rsmn=exp(-t1/(N*tamn));
for i=1:N, % correlation functions
hR(i)=2*(cos((i-1)*a))/N;
hI(i)=-2*(sin((i-1)*a))/N;
end;
ns=max(size(x_k)); % number of input data
j=1;
% main time loop
for i=1:ns,

4.3 Phasor-based Algorithms 137
dx=x_k(i);
if i>N,
dx=dx-x_k(i-N); % difference of signal
end;
if i>1,
XR(i)=XR(i-1)+hR(j)*dx; % full-period Fourier
XI(i)=XI(i-1)+hI(j)*dx; % recursive algorithm
Xa(i)=Xa(i-1)+dx; % dc component
if abs(Xa(i-1))>0,
rs(i)=Xa(i)/Xa(i-1);
if (rs(i)>1)|(rs(i)<0),
rs(i)=1;
elseif rs(i)<rsmn,
rs(i)=rsmn;
end,
else,
rs(i)=1;
end;
else,
XR(i)=hR(i)*dx; % first step
XI(i)=hI(i)*dx;
Xa(i)=x_k(i);
rs(i)=1;
end;
p=(1-rs(i))/(1+rs(i)*(rs(i)-2*cos(a)));
pc=p*(cos(a)-rs(i));
ps=p*sin(a);
del_c(i)=(pc*hR(j)+ps*hI(j))*Xa(i); % corrections
del_s(i)=(ps*hR(j)-pc*hI(j))*Xa(i);
Xc(i)=XR(i)-del_c(i);
Xs(i)=XI(i)+del_s(i);
j=j+1;
if j>N,
j=1;
end;
end; %i
return;

the correction of the DC component is fully effective after one period from the
fault point.

4.3 Phasor-based Algorithms 139
The steady-state performance of the algorithm is certainly the same as for the
standard full-period Fourier filter (Fig. 4.10). It is possible to synthesize the half-
cycle version of this algorithm, however, it is more sensitive to higher harmonics
in the input current [250].
4.3.3 Synchrophasors
A synchrophasor (synchronized phasor) is a relatively new term that is related to
the technique of phasor measurements that occur at ‘the same time’ in many
places inside the power system. Therefore, synchrophasors are the time-stamped
phasors. The synchronization process and the phasors measurement are realized in
devices generally called phasor measurement units (PMU) that may be autono-
mous or integrated in other control devices, such as a relay, a recorder etc., [236].
The big progress in the synchrophasors technique application in power systems
was made after an easy available time-synchronizing signal appeared. In the mod-
ern application the common time source (so-called universal time clock - UTC) is
delivered by the satellite global positioning system (GPS)6 in the form of a radio
clock that guarantees a time resolution less than 1 µs that allows for phase-angle
measurements with uncertainties of less than 0.02° [16]. In the standard applica-
tion the synchrophasors measure voltages and currents at diverse locations on a
power grid, and can output accurately time-stamped voltage and current phasors.
Because these phasors are truly synchronized, comparison of a few quantities is
possible in real time.
For utilizing the idea of synchrophasors it is required to respect some assumed
standard agreements. First, it is assumed that the considered continuous-time sig-
nal model is referred to the cosinusoidal function:
( )
x(t)=Xcos(ωt+ψ)=Re 2Xejωt (4.121)
where the phasor magnitude is rescaled to the RMS value:
X X
X = ejψ= ∠ψ=X +jX (4.122)
R I
2 2
The idea of the synchrophasors consists in representation of the measured
phasor by its RMS: X/√2 and an angle for each reporting request. The rates of re-
quested reports are also standardized to the maximum rate of 25 per second for a
50-Hz system and 30 rates per second for a 60-Hz system [107]. The value of an
angle reported is limited to ±π as is shown in Fig. 4.17 [242].

For fulfillment of the high-accuracy requirement of synchrophasors the signal-
processing procedures should be prepared very carefully taking into account the
following details [16, 151, 242]:
• estimation of a phasor angle and a magnitude is influenced by the system fre-
quency which may differ from the nominal value;
• the measurements need to be stable and accurate even during dynamical
changes due to sub-synchronous oscillation power swings and other low-
frequency transients;
• the measurement chain, including instrument transformers, transducers, analog
filters and A/C devices are not ideal and adequate non-linear and dynamical
corrections are needed;
• fast communication channels are needed to accommodate the data-transfer rates
required for state updates that would reflect transients.
Some of the above-mentioned problems are not so far fully resolved. For ex-
ample, it is not clear what phasor definition should be implemented during dy-
namic conditions [242, 347].
From the point of view of the applications considered here the synchrophasors
technology delivers very powerful tools that are especially important for improv-
ing the fault-location accuracy in lines with application of both-side measure-
ments. The methodology and examples are provided in Chap. 7.

4.4 Time-domain Analysis      141
4.4 Time-domain Analysis
The signal and network parameters estimation algorithms presented so far are
based on the phasor concept. They were derived on an assumption that the post-
fault state can be considered as a steady-state one. Consequently, fault-loop volt-
age and current are represented in a form of sinusoidal waveforms. However, there
are some processes in which the important information about the system parame-
ters is contained in decaying components with different frequency, including DC
component. If such transients last a relatively long period then the phasor-based
signal models may not be adequate to be the equivalent of the process. In that
situation we can try to use directly the instantaneous-based state of the system rep-
resentation.
4.4.1 Differential-equation-based Approach

approach the fault-loop model is described as a time-domain process. The model
parameters are involved with instantaneous current and voltage waveforms meas-
ured at the substation known also as the system-model-based approach.

For selection of the value of M we should take into consideration that the LSM
algorithm approximates the considered process assuming that the parameters are

and voltage signals. In this case some short-window smoothing filter is used at the
input of the procedure.

This approach can also be applied for a complex network. In the case of a

It should be noted that the algorithms originating from the system-model ap-

component does not introduce the addition error in the estimates.

4.5 Time-frequency Analysis
Standard procedures for measurement of electrical signals that represent voltage,
current and other physical values are based on the assumption that the observed
process is stable. We have shown in previous sections that such an assumption
leads to application of a well-defined Fourier transform. One of the important and
usable consequences of such an approach is easy interpretation of the measure-
ments in AC system: voltage and current phasors may be directly used for calcula-
tion of other convenient electrical parameters, such as impedance or power. There
are known, however, limitations of such a proposition: the method is not suitable
for transient period analysis and results in relatively big errors, especially when
we need to obtain a fast result.
In this section we present the wavelet transform (WT), which is well adjusted
to non-stationary signals and, moreover, has good time resolution. We further
show (Chap. 9) that this transformation may be used for fault location.
4.5.1 Short-time Fourier Transform
The aim of the signal analysis in measurements and control devices is to extract
usable information through adequate transformation. As we have seen (Sect. 4.2)
the general Fourier transform has a known practical limitation: the accurate infor-
mation about the signal spectrum (in the frequency domain) needs the information

4.5 Time-frequency Analysis 147
about the signal waveform in an unlimited time period, so we can say that it is per-
fectly local in frequency, but is global (unlimited) in time. We should also assure
that the signal is stationary. Any change observed in the signal will be averaged in
its spectrum and the information about its time inception (when it appears) will be
lost. That feature is characterized as the signal resolution in time and frequency
domains. For the Fourier transform a temporal characteristic of the signal, such as
the start and end of a finite signal and the instant of appearance of a singularity in
a transient signal, are not preserved in the spectrum.
The Fourier spectrum analysis is global in time and is practically not suitable to
analyze non-stationary and fast-changing transient signals. However, any signal
that we are interested in is of finite extent. Practically used time-restricted Fourier
transformations (as the DFT) also have limitations because transients in the data
window are averaged in the transformation process. The intention to recover the
usable information on the signal spectrum (magnitude of specified component) has
limited value because we lose information on the time of occurrence.
The above-mentioned problem is the issue of time-frequency analysis that is
based on the assumption that non-stationary signals (with varying parameters in
time) require a tool that transforms a signal into a joint time-frequency domain
[30, 246]. One such tool is known as the short time Fourier transform (STFT). It is
based on the assumption that the non-stationary signal x(t) can be divided into
segments limited by a window w(t) inside which it can be considered as the sta-
tionary one. STFT is defined as the Fourier transform of the function:
x(t)w(t−τ):
+∞
X (jω,τ)=∫ x(t)w(t−τ)e−jωtdt (4.138)
w −∞
where: w(t)=0 for t<0 and t>t .
w
As the window function w(t) is shifted in time: w(t−τ), the above transform
describes evolution of the signal spectrum with time. Generally, the window func-
tion w(t) can assume different forms but mostly it has rectangular shape.
The window function can also be connected with the complex exponential
function in (4.138) giving so-called windowed basis functions:
ψ (t)=w(t−τ)e−jωt (4.139)
ω,τ
with two parameters: the shifting coefficient τ and the frequency ω. The basis
functions represent cosine/sine waveforms of limited length with an envelope
formed by the window function. These set of functions can be used for approxima-
tion of the signal spectrum according to (4.138).

We can see that in the STFT method the frequency resolution is uniform at all
frequencies. This means that the accuracy is poor for low frequencies and be-
comes increasingly better at high frequencies. The same window length is used for
low and high spectrum analysis. The STFT, therefore, does not provide uniform
accuracy for all frequencies and the computational resources are somehow poorly
distributed.
4.5.2 Wavelet Transform
The wavelet transform concept is very similar to the above-presented STFT
method. The main difference is with new formulation of the basis functions that
are known as wavelets and are defined as:

The wavelet is an oscillating waveform that persists for only one or a few cy-
cles and, generally, is a complex-valued function. A given wavelet has a location τ
(position) and a scale p (duration), and an oscillation (frequency). Wavelets are
used as a kernel function in an integral transform, in much the same way that
complex exponentials are used in the Fourier analysis:

The relation (4.142) represents a so-called continuous wavelet transform – CWT,
because p and τ are continuous parameters.
Wavelets with different p, τ parameters create a wavelet family with a basic
(mother) wavelet ψ (t)[30]. In contrast to the Fourier transform, WT is scaled

functions that characterize degree of similarities between the signal and particular
wavelets. We can say that the signal x(t) is spread into the set of wavelets. The re-

For a given scale p transform (4.142) represents a digital filter (realized as cor-
relation) the impulse function of which is defined by an adequate wavelet. It is a
band-pass filter with medium frequency defined by the scale coefficient p. We can
see from (4.142) that a high value of p (p>>1) is related to a slow oscillating func-
tion ψ (t) with a long data window, while small values of scale p (0< p<1)

Recently, many researchers have put their efforts to use wavelet transform in
application in power engineering. Possible use of wavelet transform in power en-
gineering applications may be, but are not limited to:
• transient signal analysis and identification,
• non-stationary voltage distortion analysis,
• power-system protection – fault detection, identification, location, etc.;
• power-quality analysis and monitoring (integrated characterization of voltage
disturbances, e.g., transients, harmonics, sags);
• power-system transient data compression and storage;
• power-system analysis in general; and
• analyzing the behavior of devices, apparatus and systems.
The presented consideration is only a brief introduction into wavelet transfor-
mation issues. Generally, wavelet analysis is becoming a common tool for analyz-
ing localized transients of the observed process represented by signals and shows
the advantage of measuring transients. Some application examples are presented
in Chap. 9.

5 Measurement Chains of Fault Locators
Abstract This chapter is focused on the measurement chains of fault locators.
Transient performance of capacitive voltage transformers and their dynamic com-
pensation are considered. The basics for current transformers including the effects
of the possible saturation of current transformers are discussed. Frequency charac-
teristics of both capacitive voltage transformers and current transformers are pre-
sented. Design of analog low-pass anti-aliasing filters is addressed.
5.1 Introduction
Information on a fault, which is an abnormal power-system state, is brought to a
fault locator by its input signals. Under power-system faults the current and volt-
age signals undergo changes with respect to both steady and transient states. These
signals with the abrupt steady-state level change, and additionally being contami-
nated with the transient components, are delivered to fault-locator inputs via the
measuring chains.
The functional structure of voltage and current measurement chains of a fault
locator is shown in Fig. 5.1. Three-phase primary voltages (u ) and currents (i )
p p
from a power system are transformed with use of instrument voltage and current
transformers to the reduced secondary level (u, i). The secondary signals of these
s s
transformers are rated at around 100 V (voltage) and 1 A or 5 A (current). Then,
matching transformers provide adequate level of the signals to electronic devices.
Prior to an analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion, analog low-pass anti-aliasing fil-
ters are used for both voltage and current signals. Explanation on why such filters
have to be applied is given in Sect. 5.4. At the outputs of A/D converters the sam-
pled signals: u , i are obtained. These signals are processed in digital fault-
2(n) 2(n)
location algorithms.
Since in the majority of real applications, traditional electromagnetic voltage
and current instrument transformers are utilized, the attention in this book is given
to them. Moreover, there is a common opinion that a long time is still to pass be-
fore new unconventional instrument transformers [172, 173, 175, 220] become
pre-dominant in transforming signals from a power system to protection, monitor-
ing, control and measuring devices.

Due to certain construction limitations, both the instrument voltage (VTs) and
current (CTs) transformers exhibit undesired dynamic behavior under short cir-
cuits in the power system. As a result, malfunctioning or substantial delay in the
tripping of a protective relay may take place [72, 99, 100, 112, 154, 271, 317,
334]. Undesired steady-state and dynamic behavior of instrument transformers in-
fluence a fault-location process as well [5, 123, 232, 245, 271, 332].
Great efforts have been taken towards compensating the protective current and
voltage instrument transformers for their transient errors. The aim of such com-
pensation is to obtain a reasonably accurate replica of the primary current and
voltage. The other possibility is based on minimizing the influence of transient er-
rors of instrument transformers on the operation of both relaying and fault-
location algorithms.
5.2 Voltage Transformers
At the transmission voltage level the instrument-level voltage signals for protec-
tive, monitoring and measuring devices are provided by means of capacitive volt-
age transformers (CVTs). A CVT provides a cost-effective way of obtaining a
secondary voltage for HV and EHV systems [154, 161, 318]. Its functional
scheme is depicted in Fig. 5.2. In this scheme, besides the primary (u ) and secon-

5.2.1 Transient Performance
The dynamics of a CVT is determined by two factors [112, 154]:
• non-linear oscillations under saturation of a magnetic core of a CVT step-down
inductive voltage transformer; and
• discharging of a CVT internal energy during short circuits on the associated
transmission line.
Non-linear oscillations can appear when the operating point of the magnetizing
characteristic of the step-down transformer is shifted to the saturation region.
CVTs are therefore equipped with special anti-ferroresonance circuit (Fig. 5.3) for
avoiding stabilization of the sub-harmonics and assuring adequately fast damping
of the oscillations [161, 333]. Examples of waveforms of CVT secondary voltage
under interruption of the short-circuit of the secondary terminals are shown in
Figs. 5.4 and 5.5. For a CVT unequipped with an anti-ferroresonance circuit
(Fig. 5.4) considerable contamination with the third sub-harmonic component is
observed. Equipping a CVT with properly designed anti-ferroresonance circuit al-
lows effective damping of non-linear oscillations (Fig. 5.5). Sustained sub-
harmonic oscillations do not appear and adequately high speed of damping of os-
cillations is assured by use of a correctly designed anti-ferroresonance circuit.

Anti-ferroresonance circuits, however, affect the transients of the second kind.
Discharging the CVT internal energy (accumulated in the stack capacitors and the
compensating reactor of a CVT during the pre-fault state) – to the level that is de-
termined by the reduced fault primary voltage – results in considerable distortion
of the secondary wave [99, 112, 154, 161, 165, 266, 269].
The higher the reduction of the primary voltage, the more extensive transients
induced by the CVT itself occur (Figs. 5.6 and 5.7). In particular, faults at zero
crossing of the primary voltage result in substantial transient errors that, in turn,
affect the operation of supplied protective relays and fault locators. CVT tran-
sients may occur during changes in system-operating states either due to normal
switching operations or due to the occurrence of faults.

Among different CVT parameters, the stack capacitances influence considera-
bly the CVT-generated transients. Two types of CVT are distinguished in refer-
ence [154]:
• ‘high-C CVT’ – the sum of stack capacitances below some 100 nF; and
• ‘extra high-C CVT’ – the sum of stack capacitances above some 100 nF.
Typical CVT-generated transients for these CVT types are shown in Figs. 5.6
and 5.7. A detailed analysis of these transients is not given in this book but can be
found in [154].
In Fig. 5.6 the case for which the primary voltage drops from the rated level to
zero (for a solid fault at the primary terminals), under zero crossing, is presented.
The CVT secondary voltage also tends to zero, however, after dissipating the CVT
accumulated internal energy. The shape of the transient voltage depends highly on
the stack capacitance value. For the high-C CVT, the transient voltage assumes
higher values, but decays faster. In turn, for the extra high-C CVT, the transient
voltage assumes lower values and decays much slower.
The case for which the primary voltage drops from the rated level to zero
(a solid fault at the primary terminals) from the voltage peak is presented in
Fig. 5.7. Decay of the transient voltage is now somehow faster than in the case
presented in Fig. 5.6.

The frequency characteristics of the measuring devices are of concern mainly
when traveling-wave or high-frequency methods are considered.
The frequency response of a capacitive voltage transformer can be measured or
calculated by including the stray capacitances into the equivalent circuit diagram.
In Fig. 5.16 a typical frequency characteristic of a capacitive voltage transformer
[161] is presented. Only within some range of frequencies around the fundamental
frequency is the gain close to unity (0 dB).

In contrast to capacitive voltage transformers, current transformers have a fre-

5.3 Current Transformers
5.3.1 Basics of Current Transformers
Instrument current transformers (CTs) transform power-system currents to the
secondary level rated typically at 1 A or 5 A. The CT secondary current is sub-
stantially proportional to the primary current under normal conditions of opera-
tion, and differs in phase from it by an angle that is approximately zero for an ap-
propriate direction of the connections. The steady-state error of a CT is classified
into two: the current or ratio error, and the phase error. Both steady-state and tran-
sient performance of CTs is covered by the IEC Standard, as well as by national
standards.
Figure 5.17 depicts a CT circuit model [160, 318], which includes:

Fig. 5.17 Generic CT circuit model
CTs are designed to operate under load conditions, i.e., on the lower part of the
linear region of the U–I characteristic of the magnetizing branch. The knee point
of the magnetizing characteristic divides it into the linear and the non-linear re-
gions. The knee-point voltage is understood as the point on the magnetizing curve
where an increase of 10% in the flux density (voltage) causes an increase of 50%
in the magnetizing force (current). For high fault primary currents without the DC
component, the operating point remains in the linear range without exceeding the
knee point of the characteristic. However, if the fault conditions are such that the
DC component is present in the CT primary current, then a considerable increase
of a flux in the CT magnetic core can take place. As a consequence of such an in-
crease of a flux, the CT magnetic core gets saturated. Also, CTs can retain the re-
manent flux that may be left on the core after the fault is cleared [72, 141, 142,
349]. The remanent flux can either oppose or aid the build-up of the CT core flux,
depending on the remanent flux polarity.
When a CT gets saturated, its secondary signal becomes distorted and a high
transformation error appears. An example of waveforms of primary and secondary
currents under CT transient saturation is shown in Fig. 5.18. It can be observed
that there are intervals in which the recalculated secondary current differs consid-
erably from the primary current.
Besides transient saturation CTs may suffer permanent saturation, under which
there is no linear CT transformation at all.

5.3.2 Fault Location Under CT Saturation
Many studies related to the analysis of the steady-steady and transient behavior of
CTs have been reported so far in numerous references. The focus of attention is
the problem of how distorted secondary currents due to CT saturation can cause
malfunction or operating delays of protection relays and how to prevent saturation
or to design protective algorithms insensitive to the effects of saturation [26, 334].
An issue of fault location in relation to CT saturation has been considered as well
[332].
The remedies for assuring adequately high accuracy under CT saturation can be
categorized as follows:
• use of hardware means for preventing CT saturation [22];
• use of voltage signals alone [23, 24, 184, 233, 341];
• use of voltage signals and current signals, but excluding currents from saturated
CTs [123, 232, 271];
• minimizing fault-location errors caused by CT saturation and application of
digital algorithms for reconstructing the CT primary current [142, 145, 182,
245]; and
• allowing currents from saturated CTs to be used but only from intervals of lin-
ear transformation (when there is no saturation) [152].

5.3 Current Transformers 173
All the remedies listed, except an intentional use of voltage signals alone, re-
quire identifying the CT saturation. In general, the CT saturation identification
(detection) is understood as recognizing instants when the saturation starts and
when it ends. For this purpose saturation detectors are utilized. In general, we dis-
tinguish two families of methods for saturation detection:
• hardware-oriented methods based on superimposing an extra low power, and
high-frequency signal to the secondary circuit of a CT and monitoring the core
inductance using the superimposed signal (the value of the inductance indicates
whether or not and to what degree the supervised CT is saturated); and
• waveform-oriented methods based on analyzing only the waveform of the sec-
ondary current of a CT.
Hardware-oriented Methods
McLaren et al. [208] proposed a scheme in which a 15-kHz signal is superim-
posed to the secondary current of a CT. The apparent impedance for this signal
depends directly on the incremental inductance of the CT core, and consequently,
on the degree of saturation. Therefore, the amplitude of the high-frequency current
driven by an external voltage source acts as the saturation detector.
A similar approach was presented by Sanderson et al. in [290]. The authors use
a 10-kHz externally driven signal to monitor the value of the equivalent magnetiz-
ing inductance of a CT. Keeping the 10-kHz driving force constant, the authors use a
10-kHz current as the indicator of saturation.
The obvious disadvantage of this family of methods is the need for connecting
an extra circuit between the main CTs and the relay (fault locator). However, as
measuring directly an equivalent magnetizing inductance of a CT, these methods
appear as very robust.
Waveform-oriented Methods
The methods from this group process directly the waveform of the CT secondary
current in order to distinguish between the linear and saturated operation of a CT.
They are investigated as numerical procedures to be run exclusively on digital re-
lays and fault locators. They call for comparatively high sampling frequencies in
order to assure adequately short delays in detecting instants when a saturation
starts and when it stops. Let us present two further examples of saturation detec-
tors of this kind proposed in [152] and the modal saturation detector [103]. An-
other saturation detector that is based on processing the secondary current with
use of an algorithm that evaluates the first, second and third difference functions is
presented in [143, 144].

The method from [103] has two distinctive features compared with the previ-

immunity to CT saturation appearing only at one line end [123]. Such a fault-

grossly contaminated due to CT saturation, has to be rejected.

Adaptive Measuring Technique
There is a chance that CT saturation, if it occurs, is a transient saturation only. In
such a situation, in every cycle of the fundamental frequency, the CTs show peri-
ods of linear transformation. If a saturation detector is capable of indicating such
periods, information brought by the samples from the linear operation of CTs may
be used for determining criteria quantities, such as: amplitude of current, resis-
tance, reactance, more accurately than by use of the standard Fourier technique
[152].
However, the periods of saturation-free CT transformation may be quite short.
Therefore, the use of variable data window techniques was recommended in [152].
In a variable data window algorithm, the data window extends after activation of
the measurement and when it reaches its pre-defined full length (N samples) it
stops extending and starts to slide. This technique, which combines both detection
of saturated/linear operation of a CT and the variable data window measuring al-
gorithm, is further named the adaptive method (Figs. 5.22 and 5.23).
As a result of applying the variable data window measuring algorithm one
earns ultra-high-speed response of a measuring algorithm due to removing pre-
fault samples from the data window. Deterioration of the filtration quality of such
an algorithm is the price to pay for this gain [331, 336].

The impedance (R, X) is measured based upon orthogonal components of both
voltage (u) and current (i) signals. Voltage can be processed using a constant
width data window (for example the full-cycle Fourier), while current signal is
split into its orthogonal components using the adaptive method (5.19) and (5.20).
Since the voltage data window slides, thus its midpoint moves by one sample. On
the other hand, the data window for a current extends, thus its midpoint moves by
half a sample. Therefore, an appropriate phase-compensating procedure must be
applied. The group delay assumes:

Figure 5.23 presents an example performance of the adaptive algorithm for
measuring current magnitude. In comparison to the full-cycle Fourier algorithm
the adaptive algorithm provides much better response, both faster time response
and better steady-state accuracy. Similarly, measurement of resistance and reac-
tance (Fig. 5.24) appears superior with use of the adaptive method. Features of the
presented adaptive method indicate the possibility of directly applying it to im-
pedance-based fault-location algorithms [109, 352]. Successful application of this
method to overcurrent relays is reported in [26], and to distance relays in [334].

Hardware Methods for Compensating Distortion in Secondary Current
Besides digital algorithms, analog (hardware) methods for compensating the dis-
tortion in the secondary current have also been developed.
In [22], an analog circuit is connected to the secondary terminals of a CT and
used to generate a DC component equal and opposite to that seen in the primary
one. Then, by injecting the generated DC component into the secondary winding
component prevents saturation of a CT.
A digital algorithm for compensating the secondary current is put forward in
[145]. Then, an advanced compensating algorithm of the distorted secondary
current immune to the remanent flux is proposed in [141,142]. These algorithms
estimate the secondary current corresponding to the CT ratio under CT satura-
tion using the flux–current curve. In addition, it is stated that this approach al-
lows for successful compensation of the secondary current even when a smaller
CT than the rated size is used, resulting in secondary currents being more se-
verely distorted. Moreover, it is shown [141, 142] that the proposed compensat-
ing algorithm can be implemented in real time into a digital-signal-processor
hardware as part of the main protective relaying algorithm.

5.4 Analog Anti-aliasing Filters
The sampling of analog signals is performed with use of A/D converters. Digital
information contained in the set of samples obtained differs from that provided by
analog signals [230, 298]. The digital frequency is equal to the analog frequency if
the frequency of the sampled analog signal is smaller than half of the sampling
frequency (0.5f). This threshold value is commonly called the Nyquist frequency.
s
Sampling the sine analog wave of the frequency higher than this threshold value

5.4 Analog Anti-aliasing Filters 183
results in obtaining a set of samples that represent the sine wave of the frequency
different from that at the input of the A/D converter. Figure 5.26 shows the digital
frequency versus the analog frequency.
Suppose that the calculations are based on fundamental frequency (f ) compo-

different frequencies: f , f – f , f + f , 2f – f , 2f + f , …, after sampling give sets

of sinusoids changing frequency during sampling is called aliasing. The term
‘aliasing’ is originated here from comparing the effect of the frequency change to
the crime on an identity (an alias), which is understood here as the frequency of an
analog sine wave. In addition to the frequency-change effect, the aliasing also
changes the phase of the signal by π for the respective ranges of frequencies of the
analog signal, as shown in Fig. 5.27.
