Using the first-order (Fig. 5.30) and the second-order (Fig. 5.31) Sallen–Key
low-pass circuits one can build higher-order anti-aliasing analog filters. Another
option in this respect is use of the switched capacitor filters, which are composed
of capacitors and electronic switches.
Design of the analog anti-aliasing filter with the given cut-off frequency re-
quires assuming the respective standard approximation of the transfer function and
its order. Three types of analog filters are commonly used: Butterworth, Cheby-
shev, and Bessel (also called a Thompson filter) [298]. A transfer function of each
of them is obtained as a result of optimizing a different performance parameter.
There is a wide literature on this subject.

6 One-end Impedance-based Fault-location
Algorithms
Abstract In this chapter, a variety of one-end impedance-based fault-location al-
gorithms are presented. The algorithms presented are designed for locating faults
on single-circuit lines, double-circuit lines, and series-compensated lines. Both
transposed and untransposed lines are taken into consideration. The algorithms are
formulated for the lumped-line models. The chapter is concluded with the intro-
duction of a distributed-parameter line model for improving fault-location accu-
racy.
6.1 Introduction
The one-end fault-location algorithms are simple and economical, when compared
with two-end methods and those based on the traveling-wave and high-frequency
component techniques. These algorithms are designed for estimating the location
of transmission-line faults with use of three-phase current and voltage measured at
one terminal of a line. Also, there are some algorithms that utilize three-phase vol-
tage or current alone. The fundamental frequency phasors of the measured signals
or the sampled data are processed in the algorithms. Also the impedance parame-
ters of the network are required for determining a distance to fault.
6.2 Fault Location Based on Impedance Measurement
The impact of fault resistance on one-end impedance measurement is a key factor
in deriving the majority of one-end fault-location algorithms. Let us start with
considering a single-phase line (A–B) connected to a source at one end (A) only,
i.e., the line that supplies no load at the end B (Fig. 6.1). The line is affected by a
fault (F), which is at unknown distance d (p.u.) from the bus A, where the fault lo-
cator (FL) is installed. If the line charging current is neglected, then the current at
the fault locator (I ) is equal to the current at the fault (I ). The impedance seen
A F
from the fault-locator terminal, calculated using the voltage U and current I , is:

6.3 Fault Current Distribution Factors      191
The fault-location algorithm (6.8) was derived for a single-phase line. For
three-phase lines, the symmetrical-components or phase-coordinates approaches
are considered in successive sections of this chapter.

In formula (6.33), the angle of the current distribution factor (for the positive-

equals zero (γ = 0), i.e., that the fault current distribution factor is a real number.
In practice, this assumption is not completely fulfilled and thus there is a certain
error due to this. However, in the case of a high-voltage network these additional
errors are not substantial, as reported in [106, 330].

6.7 Fault Location with Use of Impedance Data of Network
An accurate one-end fault-location algorithm has been introduced by Eriksson et
al. [62]. The fault-location algorithm uses novel compensation techniques for the
errors resulting from remote source infeed into the fault resistance. This is accom-
plished by using a complete network model. The actual distribution of a fault cur-
rent in the transmission network is taken into account. Compensation for fault re-
sistance voltage drop utilizes pre-fault current and representative values for source
resistance and reactance. This inclusion of source impedances is a novel approach.
In [62], it introduced into (6.34) the following form for the fault current distri-
bution factor for the positive- (negative-) sequence:

206 6 One-end Impedance-based Fault-location Algorithms
The remote source impedance Z as shown in Table 6.1 is the other parameter
1B
required by the fault-location formula (6.44). This impedance can be determined
on condition that the exact network topology and parameters are known. Other-
wise, its ‘representative’ value has to be provided as the input data [62]. Some
mismatch between the actual impedance and the provided ‘representative’ can ap-
pear. However, in strong meshed modern networks the equivalent system configu-
ration is fixed [233] and the expected mismatch is rather not too high. Moreover,
it follows from the many years’ of operational experiences [62] in more than 100
countries around the world that the mismatch causes no problem. So, the need for
providing the remote source impedance (Z ) cannot be considered as the algo-
1B
rithm limitation. On the contrary, the representative values of remote source im-
pedance provide improved accuracy.
On the other hand, there is a possibility [93] for improving fault-location accu-
racy by sending the source impedance, which can be measured at the remote end
devices (for example, in the recording device RD), with use of simple and even
slow communication means (Fig. 6.7).

Example 6.1 Fault location according to the fault-location algorithm from [62]
Figure 6.8 presents an example of fault location on a single 400-kV, 300-km line
for the following fault specifications:
– fault type: a–g;
– fault resistance: 10 Ω;
– fault location: 0.7 p.u.
The estimated fault distance (averaged over the time interval lasting from
30 ms up to 50 ms after the fault inception) equals 0.7079 p.u., and thus the error
is 0.8%. The accuracy obtained can be improved by introducing the compensation
for the line shunt capacitances (Sect. 6.15).

The first algorithm from [52] covers only the faults for which an earth is in-
volved and thus the zero-sequence current is present. For the phase-to-phase fault
one can formulate a relation between the incremental positive- and negative-
sequence currents – the second algorithm from [52]. However, the distance to
fault can be determined from this relation only for specific conditions with imped-
ances of the network for the positive- and negative-sequence being not identical.
Normally, this is not so and the fault current distribution factors for the incre-
mental positive- and negative-sequence involved in the relation, being identical
are cancelled and the relation becomes useless.
Evaluation of the fault-location accuracy performed in [52] has shown the
presence of relatively big errors. Fortunately, the errors do not depend on fault re-
sistance and pre-fault power-flow direction. Therefore, one can apply the correc-
tion factors, calculated in advance, for correcting the results obtained for the par-
ticular line and network topology. The other possibility is to derive the relation
formula (3.3) taking into account the distributed-parameter line model.
The fault-location method discussed does not cover all faults, and thus cannot
be considered as the only one suitable for implementing into the fault locator. It
can be used as the supplement of other methods. Due to the simplicity of the algo-
rithm, it can be utilized not only for fault location (off-line application), but also in
the field of distance protection (on-line application).

age phasors [109]. For this purpose, the symmetrical components of the measured

Non-standard use of one-terminal measurements of voltage and current for
fault location was presented in [233]. Voltage phasors from the fault interval only
are required, while the current phasors only from the pre-fault time, when CT sa-
turation does not occur. When use is made of such input signals, the CT saturation
does not affect the fault-location accuracy. The algorithm covers all faults. It re-
quires impedances of equivalent systems at both line terminals to be known, as
well as performing the fault classification, assuming at the same time that the fault
impedance is purely resistive.
The solution in [233] consists in comparing the voltage measured at the local
terminal (A) with the calculated one, taking into account the objective function of
the sum of errors modules:

6.12 Fault Location with Arc-voltage Estimation      221
Node voltages under fault condition are calculated [233] using three-phase in-

phase nodal admittance matrix.
Unknown fault distance (d) and fault resistance (R F ) are obtained through an
optimization algorithm at the point of minimum of function (6.67).
6.12 Fault Location with Arc-voltage Estimation
The arcing character of faults is reflected in the algorithms presented in [51, 54].
This numerical algorithm is based on one terminal data and is derived in the time
domain. The fault location and its nature, in terms of arcing or arc-less fault, are
estimated using the least error squares technique. The faulted phase voltage (Fig.
6.16) is modeled as a serial connection of fault resistance (R ) and arc voltage (u)
F
– represented by the model defined in formula (3.11). The algorithm is derived for
the most frequent case of a single phase-to-ground fault.

After transforming (6.68) into the discrete form, an estimation with the use of

Besides the basic feature of the algorithm relying on determining the nature of
the fault the distance to fault is also obtained. Moreover, the approach does not re-
quire the line zero-sequence resistance as input data.
6.13 Fault Location on Untransposed Lines
The symmetrical components approach can be effectively used for locating faults
on completely symmetrical lines, i.e., on transposed lines. However, the symmetry
of a line can be substantially disturbed, which is the case when there are long
segments of a line without transposition of the conductors (untransposed line).
The other causes are related with such installations as, for example, series-
compensating capacitors equipped with MOVs for overvoltage protection, which
introduce asymmetry upon the occurrence of unsymmetrical faults.
In order to take into account the asymmetry of a line, the phase coordinates ap-
proach [109, 216, 274, 284] will be applied for representing a faulted line in the
fault-location algorithm. The voltage drop across a three-phase element, represented
by a column matrix of three-phase voltage U, can be expressed as a product of an
impedance matrix (Z) and a column matrix of measured three-phase current (I):

In [109], a quantitative evaluation of the fault-location accuracy, with use of
ATP-EMTP [56] generated fault data has been performed. It was shown that for
the transmission system studied there, the presented algorithm allows the fault-
location accuracy to be improved up to 2%, compared to the symmetrical compo-
nents approach (applied after averaging the diagonal and off-diagonal elements of
the line-impedance matrix). Note that such an improvement was obtained for
comparatively small asymmetry of the line under consideration [109]. In the pres-
ence of larger asymmetry of the line, the improvement can be considerably higher.
6.14 Fault Location on Series-compensated Lines
Installation of SC and MOV banks (series capacitors (SCs) and their overvoltage
protective devices MOVs) in series-compensated lines causes some difficulties for
fault location. First, the presence of SC and MOV banks has to be reflected in the
fault-location algorithms. Also, the detection at which line section (in front or be-
hind the compensating bank) a fault occurred appears as an important issue.
6.14.1 Representation of Compensating Bank
Series capacitors equipped with MOVs (Fig. 6.21) create certain problems for
transmission-line protective devices and fault locators. In order to cope with them,

228 6 One-end Impedance-based Fault-location Algorithms
adequate representations of SCs and MOVs have to be developed, being required
for both distance-protection and fault-location purposes.

The fundamental frequency concept has been utilized for representing SCs and
MOVs for fault-location purposes in [111, 274]. In turn, a digital algorithm for es-
timating a voltage drop across the bank of SC and MOV has been considered for
application to fault location in [254] and for protective relaying purposes in [277].
This estimation algorithm is based on the on-line solving of the strongly non-
linear differential equation and is of recursive form.

The algorithm is accurate and numerically efficient owing to the following fac-
tors [277]:
•
The difference in the signal levels (voltage is in thousands while current is in
tens or hundreds) is removed by applying the p.u. value of the voltage drop.
•  The strong non-linearity of the equation is moderated by using either of the two
optimal formulae: (6.88) or (6.89), depending on the operating point on the
characteristic of the MOV.
•
The algorithm ensures satisfactory accuracy for time steps as large as 1/20th of
the fundamental frequency cycle (it needs 2–3 iterations to find a solution). For
shorter time steps (sampling frequency over 1000 Hz) the algorithm performs
even better.
It is assumed that the pre-fault current is available and the estimation algorithm
is started a posteriori, a few samples before detecting the fault. Thus, the algorithm is
initiated in the pre-fault steady state using the zero conditions, i.e., assuming:
| x =0,      x | =0    |     |     | (6.95)  |

| (n−1)        | (n−2) |     |     |         |
In the pre-fault conditions, the compensating bank is a pure capacitance (since
the MOV almost does not conduct a current) and when using the algorithm with
zero initial conditions (6.95), a certain constant offset to the accurate solution is
added. In order to remove this offset, it is recommended to apply the following
digital filter:

234 6 One-end Impedance-based Fault-location Algorithms
Implementation of the estimation algorithm, for the case where only the first
form (6.88) is utilized, into the Matlab function [202] follows. The task of incor-
porating the second form (6.89) into this Matlab function is left for the reader.
Matlab Function for Estimating Voltage Drop Across SC and MOV
function vMOVa=MOV_fun(ia); % ‘ia’ is the input current
n_iter=2; % here fixed number (2) of iterations is set
C=4.8119e-005; % capacitance of series capacitor
P=1000.0; % reference current of MOV characteristic
q=23; % exponent of MOV characteristic
V_REF=150000.0; % reference voltage of MOV characteristic
f=50; % rated power system frequency
fs=1000; % sampling frequency
omega1=2*pi*f; % rated power system angular frequency
a=omega1/fs; % angle corresp. to single sampling interval
kF=0.5/(cos(a)–1); % gain of filter for DC rejecting
D=omega1/sqrt(26–32*cos(a)+6*cos(2*a)); % const. of GEAR rule
A_q=P; % constant
A_1=3*D*C*V_REF; % constant
l=size(ia); % size of input current
x=[0;0;0]; % initial conditions
for n=1:l(1), % processing with time
A_0=ia(n)+A_1*[0 4 –1]*x/3; % from numeric formula
for k=1:n_iter, % perform iter. calculations
z=abs(x(1));
if z,
z=log(z);
z=A_q*exp(q*z);
if x(1)<0, z=–z; end;
z1=q*z/x(1);
else,
z1=0;
end;
x(1)=x(1)–(z+A_1*x(1)–A_0)/(z1+A_1);
end,
if n<4, % reject the constant offset
xF(n)=kF*[1 –2 1]*x;
end,

6.14 Fault Location on Series-compensated Lines 235
if n==3,
xF(n)=kF*[1 –2 1]*x;
x(1)=ia(n)/A_1+(4*xF(n)–xF(n–1))/3;
x(2)=xF(n);
end,
x(3)=x(2);
x(2)=x(1);
vMOVa_pu(n,1)=x(1); % result in per units
end;
vMOVa=vMOVa_pu*V_REF; % result in Volts

In the measured phase voltages (Fig. 6.25a) and phase currents (Fig. 6.25b) one
observes the characteristic distortion of the waveforms. It is distinctive that, in
contrast to the uncompensated-line case, there are no DC components in the cur-
rents. Limiting of the voltage drop across SC and MOV from the faulted phase to
the level equal to around the reference voltage of MOV (V ) is observed (Fig.
REF

which results in slowly decaying sub-harmonic oscillations (Fig. 6.25c). Figure

phase (EMTP simulation) and the signal estimated with the algorithm presented.
The accuracy of the voltage reconstruction is very high and the difference between
the actual and calculated values is very small. Note that the voltage drop is calcu-
lated at the sampling instants only (1000 Hz sampling frequency was assumed
here) and therefore the calculated voltage drop is presented as a stair waveform.

Selection Algorithm
Locating a fault with respect to the SC and MOVs in the system of Fig. 6.21, i.e.,
selecting either SUB_1 or SUB_2 as a valid subroutine, is a separate issue. Here,
however, the problem narrows to the selection of the correct pair (d, R ) out of
F
two alternatives (d , R ) and  (d , R ), as depicted in Fig. 6.29a. The simple

| ---- | ------------- | --- | ----------------------------------- | ------- | --- | --- |
|      | 1             |     | SC 2                                | SC      |     |     |

accept (d ,R ) as the valid solution, otherwise select the alternative with low-

er R  as the valid solution.
F
This selecting algorithm works in most cases. In order to avoid false selection,
which could happen in some rare cases, an additional selection criterion has been
proposed. This criterion is based on calculating currents at the fault place, accord-
ing to both subroutines: SUB_1, SUB_2, substituting the obtained distances to
fault, d , d . Ideally, for the valid subroutine the calculated currents from healthy
|     | 1   | 2   |     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
phases at fault have to be equal to zero (since in the healthy phases there is no cur-
rent flow at all). In practice, due to the presence of the errors, a certain threshold
has to be assumed for indicating that these currents are close to zero (the valid

6.14 Fault Location on Series-compensated Lines 241
subroutine) or far away from zero (the false subroutine). This criterion can be ap-
plied except in the case of three-phase faults under which there are no healthy
phases.
Summary of Data and Measurements
The algorithm needs the following data:
• line impedance (3×3 phase matrix);
• local source impedance (3×3 phase matrix);
• remote source impedance (3×3 phase matrix);
• location of the compensating bank (d ); and
SC
• equivalenting branch for the SC and MOV (two functions for R , X or tables),
v v
and the following measurements:
• type of fault;
• fault detection in terms of identifying the fault inception and clearance instants;
• three-phase local voltages (phasors); and
• three-phase local currents including their pre-fault values (phasors).
Improvements of the One-end Fault-location Algorithm
The fault algorithm has been presented in its very basic form. The important en-
hancements for its field implementation may include:
• the impedance of the local system should be traced on-line based on the se-
quence voltages and currents; owing to this, the local impedance is always per-
fectly matched;
• more involved techniques should be used for phasor estimation and dealing
with the off-nominal frequencies;
• advanced post-processing techniques for output filtering and elaborated meth-
ods for selecting the final result from the available data window should be ap-
plied;
• the remote end source impedance may also be accurately measured by the re-
mote end relays or fault locators and transmitted to the local substation; no
sampling synchronization is needed (the voltage and current act as reference
for each other); and
• the amplitude of the remote current may also be measured and transmitted ena-
bling iterative calculations to be avoided for the subroutine SUB_2 and im-
proving the accuracy.
Example 6.5 Fault-location on series-compensated line
The following specifications of the fault on a 400-kV, 300-km transmission line,
compensated at 70% rate with the three-phase compensating bank installed at the
midline (d = 0.5 p.u.) were assumed:
SC

242 6 One-end Impedance-based Fault-location Algorithms
– fault type: a–g;
– distance to fault: d = 0.5+ p.u. (just behind SCs and MOVs – the subroutine
SUB_1 is valid);
– fault resistance: R = 10 Ω.

phase total fault current (Fig. 6.30e) indicates the subroutine SUB_1 as the valid
one. The estimation error for the fault distance (from the valid subroutine SUB_1)
shown in Fig. 6.30f is definitely acceptable, as it does not exceed 0.5% after
around 1.5 fundamental-frequency cycles since fault incipience. Note: full-cycle
Fourier filtration was applied for determining the phasors of the processed signals.
6.14.3 Fault Location on Line Compensated at Both Ends
The presented earlier fault-location algorithm (for a line compensated at midline)
can be easily adapted to a line compensated at both ends (Fig. 6.31), as presented
in [272]. Taking into consideration the more difficult case with instrument trans-
formers installed on the bus side (Fig. 2.30a), one can distinguish two characteris-
tic fault positions (Fig. 6.31), as seen by the one-end fault locator installed at the
bus A:
• fault F1 on the line between the compensation banks I, II: the subroutine
SUB_1; and
• fault F2 overreaching the line length (in the remote system B): the subroutine
SUB_2.
The remote compensating bank II has different equivalents, depending on
which subroutine is considered. For the subroutine SUB_1 it is dependent on the
magnitude of the remote current I , which is unavailable for the considered one-
B

end fault locator from the substation A. Therefore, analogously as for the subrou-
tine SUB_2 of the fault-location algorithm for a line compensated with a single
compensating bank installed at midline, iterative calculations have to be per-
formed. Selection of the valid subroutine can be done utilizing the same criteria as
for a line compensated with a single compensating bank installed at midline.

6.14.4 Fault Location on Double-circuit Series-compensated Line
Fault location on a double-circuit line requires additionally taking into account a
mutual coupling effect, when adapting the fault-location algorithm, which was de-
signed for a single-circuit line. Two algorithms for application to a double-circuit
series-compensated line follow:
• basic algorithm;
• improved algorithm.
6.14.4.1 Basic Algorithm
Analogously, as for the earlier considered configurations of series-compensated
lines, there is a need for also applying two subroutines (SUB_1, SUB_2) for dou-
ble-circuit series-compensated line [284]. The final result is obtained with the se-
lection algorithm, used for indicating the valid subroutine.
Equivalent circuit diagram of double-circuit series-compensated line for the
pre-fault state is shown in Fig. 6.32. The description of this circuit is utilized for
deriving both subroutines.

6.14.5 Differential-equation-based Algorithm
In [254, 279] the one-end fault-location algorithm for a series-compensated line,
which is based on differential-equation approach has been delivered. This algo-
rithm (SUB_1diff) has been developed with the aim of applying it as the supple-
mentary subroutine to the subroutine SUB_1 (designated for locating faults behind
SCs and MOVs), formulated with use of the fundamental-frequency phasor ap-
proach. The differential-equation approach has advantages for locating faults be-
hind SCs and MOVs involving high fault resistances, i.e., for the fault cases when
the MOVs operate linearly or almost linearly, which results in an increase in
slowly decaying subharmonic components.
The fault-location algorithm based on the differential-equation approach [254,
279] utilizes a Clarke transformation (2.44) [25, 56, 254, 279].
Clarke Transformation
Transformation of the phase coordinates (in the time domain) of a 3-phase (a, b, c)
symmetrical system into the 0, α, β coordinates can be performed according to the
following matrix relation:

6.15 Accuracy Improvement by Application of Distributed-
parameter Line Model
The varieties of fault-location algorithms presented above (Sects. 6.5 and 6.14)
were derived assuming the lumped model of a transmission line and neglecting the
line shunt parameters (pre-dominantly the shunt capacitances). The fault-loop
formula (6.28) was used for deriving those algorithms. Introducing in (6.28) the
fault-loop current for the single line (6.26) one obtains the following form for the
fault-loop formula [121]:
 Z 
U −dZ a I +a I +a 0L I −R (a I +a I +a I )=0 (6.145)
A_P 1L  1 A1 2 A2 0 Z 1L A0  F F1 F1 F2 F2 F0 F0
in which there are the coefficients dependent on fault type (gathered in Table 6.5
and Tables 3.3–3.5).
Using (6.145) accurate location of faults on transmission lines of comparatively
short length can be performed. In order to keep the fault-location errors in the case
of long lines (usually considered as exceeding 150 km) on the acceptable level,
the distributed-parameter line model has to be incorporated.
The distributed-parameter model of faulted line for the ith symmetrical compo-
nent from Fig. 2.25 will be utilized for simplified introduction of the distributed-
parameter line model into the fault-loop formula (6.145). This model is simplified

6.15 Accuracy Improvement by Application of Distributed-parameter Line Model      261
(not strict) since in order to avoid solving non-linear equations, iterative calcula-
tions are performed. Performing the current iteration (the iteration number n), the
shunt parameters (capacitances) for the faulted-line section are determined not by
an accurate value of the distance to fault but by the value obtained in the last but
one iteration (the iteration number: (n – 1)). Also, the longitudinal line impedance
for the line section in the model from Fig. 2.25 is determined using the distance to
fault value obtained in the previous iteration of the calculations. In order to start
the iterative calculations, the distance to fault obtained for the lumped-line model
has to be taken.
Introducing into (6.145) the distributed-parameter line model from Fig. 2.25
one obtains:

7 Two-end and Multi-end Fault-location
Algorithms
Abstract This chapter is focused on two-end and multi-end fault-location algo-
rithms. First, the algorithms utilizing two-end synchronized measurements are
presented for both phasor-based and time-domain approaches. Then, use of the
unsynchronized measurements is considered in detail. Different options for meas-
uring the synchronization angle are introduced. Use of both complete and incom-
plete two-end measurements is considered for two-end fault-location algorithms.
Algorithms utilizing measurements of distance relays are presented. Fault location
on three-terminal and multi-terminal lines is addressed.
7.1 Introduction
With the aim of overcoming the limitations of the one-end fault-location tech-
niques and improving fault-location accuracy, two-end and multi-end fault-
location algorithms have been proposed. Use of both synchronized [29, 65, 105,
107, 132, 133, 163, 164, 190, 191, 235, 236, 294, 323, 340] and unsynchronized
[42, 116, 131, 185–187, 224–226, 297, 319, 320] measurements is considered for
these algorithms. In the case of unsynchronized measurements, different ways of
dealing with the unknown synchronization angle are presented. With regard to the
utilized measurements, the following options are of interest for the two-end fault
location:
• complete two-end measurements: three-phase voltages and currents from both
line ends; and
• incomplete two-end measurements:
– three-phase voltages from both line ends, with three-phase current from
only one end;
– three-phase currents from both line ends, with three-phase voltage from
only one end;
– three-phase voltages from both line ends.

264      7 Two-end and Multi-end Fault-location Algorithms
Use of measurements of distance relays from the line terminals is considered
for deriving fault-location algorithms, which are designed for application to post-
fault analysis of operation of the relays [120, 130, 259, 260, 270].
Also, different options with respect to the availability of measurements from
the terminals of three-terminal and multi-terminal lines are considered for use by
the fault-location algorithms.

into an ordinary differential equation.

Steps in Fault Location
Using the voltage and current profiles, calculated by means of the method of char-
acteristics, the fault-location procedure from [88] consists of the following steps:
• Modal decomposition used for obtaining three decoupled single-phase trans-
mission lines (from a three-phase coupled system), to which the method of cha-
racteristics can be applied.

7.3 Use of Two-end Unsynchronized Measurements 267
• Discretization of the transmission line: Based on the sampling frequency of the
data acquisition, each mode of the transmission line is discretized into a finite
number of points.
• Location of the approximate fault point: For each discrete point determined
above, compute the voltage due to the sending end voltage and current. Then,
the procedure using the receiving end data is repeated and the approximate
fault point is found (the point with the least error).
• Refining the fault location performed with use of reconstructed voltage and
current values transformed back to the phase domain.
7.3 Use of Two-end Unsynchronized Measurements
When the phasors of voltages and currents are obtained from digital measurements
acquired asynchronously at the line terminals, there is no common time reference.
This happens when the GPS facility is not used or for some reasons the signal
from the GPS is not received. In order to make use of such measurements for fault
location, a common time reference has to be provided. Different approaches for
that follow in the next sections. In these approaches the measurements from the
terminal B will be assumed as the base, while all phasors for voltage and current
from the end A will be multiplied by the synchronization operator ejδ, where δ is
the synchronization angle, which has to be determined or eliminated in mathemati-
cal manipulations.
7.3.1 Fault Location with Measurement of Synchronization Angle
In the case of utilizing unsynchronized measurements one may perform fault loca-
tion with use of (7.8), which is valid for synchronized measurements. However,
earlier determination of the synchronization operator ejδ and making analytical
synchronization of measurements are required.
The needed synchronization operator can be determined by utilizing the follow-
ings:
• relationships between pre-fault quantities – Sect. 7.3.1.1;
• boundary conditions of particular faults – Sect. 7.3.1.2.
In order to achieve high accuracy for determination of the synchronization op-
erator, the distributed-parameter line model for both approaches will be utilized.

7.3.1.2 Measurement of Synchronization Angle with Use of Fault Quantities
Alternatively, the synchronization operator can be determined using only fault
quantities (measured within the fault period). For this purpose, the boundary con-
ditions of particular faults can be explored [123]. In the case of three-phase bal-
anced faults, the positive-sequence components are the only ones, which are pre-
sent  in  the  measured  currents  and  voltages.  For  this  reason,  the  boundary
conditions will be considered for all faults, except for three-phase balanced faults,
for which the synchronization operator can be determined with use of pre-fault
positive-sequence quantities, i.e., by applying (7.18) or (7.21) or (7.24).

7.3.3 Analytical Determination of Synchronization Angle
In [225], a fundamental fault-location algorithm, which utilizes two-end unsyn-
chronized measurement has been introduced. It was formulated in terms of sym-
metrical components of the measured currents and voltages. Since different types
of components can be utilized, the algorithm will be presented in general form,
i.e., for the ith symmetrical component (subscript i). The algorithm from [225] is
derived starting with substitution of the synchronization operator:

In [225], (7.47) is solved iteratively, applying the Newton–Raphson method.
The iterative calculations are stopped when the difference between the last two
values of the synchronization angle is smaller than a pre-assigned limit. An initial
value for the unknown synchronization angle is required. In [225], setting the ini-
tial value to zero has been recommended. This is due to the fact that in practice,
the synchronization angle is contained within a limited range around zero. The
calculations have been observed to converge rapidly in numerous cases.
Once the synchronization angle is known, the distance to fault can be calcu-
lated from the real or imaginary part of (7.46).

The digital values for the synchronization angle (Fig. 7.7) and distance to fault
(Fig. 7.8) are singled out by averaging (subscript: av.) within the interval lasting
from 30 to 50 ms after the fault inception.
Using positive-sequence quantities the following averaged values of the syn-
chronization angle have been obtained: 94.28°, 37.42° (Fig. 7.7a), while using the
negative-sequence components: 36.11°, –143.78° (Fig. 7.7a). There are four pos-
sible  pairs  of  the  calculated  angles:  (94.28°,  36.11°);  (94.28°,  –143.78°);
(37.42°, 36.11°); (37.42°, –143.78°).

7.3 Use of Two-end Unsynchronized Measurements 281
The pair (37.42°, 36.11°) consists of the synchronization angle values that are
the closest to each other and do not differ too much. Such a pair with coincident
results indicates the valid solution for the synchronization angle. Taking the values
37.42° (for the positive-sequence) or 36.11° (for the negative-sequence), respec-
tively, the distance to fault (Fig. 7.8) was determined. In the case of using the
positive-sequence quantities one gets:
– for the lumped-line model: 0.8964 p.u.;
– for the distributed-parameter line model: 0.8003 p.u.
Applying the negative-sequence components as the fault-locator input signals,
the following results have been obtained:
– for the lumped-line model: 0.7948 p.u.;
– for the distributed-parameter line model: 0.7998 p.u.

7.3 Use of Two-end Unsynchronized Measurements 285
The voltage and current signals measured by the relays are sent to the computer
performing the analysis. Versatile methods for processing the input signals have
been included in the post-fault analysis program developed [120]. In addition, the
fault-loop impedance measurement performed in the distance relays is taken into
account. The other part of the program utilizes the fault-loop impedance meas-
urements that are based on the two-end fault-location principle. Prior to the fault
location, the processed two-end signals are analytically synchronized.
Distance relays measure the apparent impedance of the appropriate fault loop
using the relaying voltage (U ) and current (I ) signals. These signals are

Example 7.3 Fault location with analytical synchronization of measurements of
distance relays
Figures 7.12 through 7.17 present the results for the a–g fault on a 400-kV, 300-km
single-circuit transmission line. The emfs at the bus B were assumed as leading
the emfs of the side A by 30°; distance to fault from the terminal A: d = 0.8 p.u.,
fault resistance: R = 10 Ω .
F
Processing the input signals as shown in Fig. 7.12, the distance relay at the
terminal A determines the fault-loop resistance (Fig. 7.13a) and reactance
(Fig. 7.13b). Due to the presence of the reactance effect, the determined values
differ from the actual resistance and reactance of the transmission-line section
from the measuring point (A) up to the fault point (F). A full-cycle Fourier filter-
ing was applied to the measurement. Polar plots of the impedance measurements
are shown in Fig. 7.14a (for the first 20 samples) and Fig. 7.14b (for the next 20
samples). One observes that due to the reactance effect the trajectory of the meas-
ured fault-loop impedance does not enter the MHO impedance characteristic, for
which the reach of 85% of the line positive-sequence impedance was set. The re-
actance effect causes the fault occurring at 80% of the line length to be not de-
tected by the first zone MHO element set at 85%.
In turn, application of the two-end fault-location algorithm allows accurate lo-
cation of the fault. It starts with determination of the synchronization angle using
the relaying signals (fault-loop voltage and current) – Fig. 7.15a, or the negative-
sequence signals – Fig. 7.15b. This allows us to select the valid values for the syn-
chronization angle (18.47°, 18.15°), which are very close to the introduced intentional
desynchronization (δ = 18°). Performing analytical synchronization with use of the
actual
determined synchronization angle, the distance to fault (d [p.u.]) was calculated. Then,
the fault-loop impedance using the fault-location principle (Fig. 7.16) was calculated:
Z =dZ , the trajectory of which surely enters the interior of the MHO characteris-
FL 1L
tic. Figure 7.17 shows a comparison of the fault-loop resistance (Fig. 7.17a) and reac-
tance (Fig. 7.17b) determined in two different ways, according to the following
principles:
• classic distance relay measurement; and
• using the two-end fault-location principle.

298 7 Two-end and Multi-end Fault-location Algorithms
7.4 Use of Incomplete Two-end Measurements
7.4.1 Use of Two-end Voltages
A fault-location method utilizing synchronized measurements of two-end voltages
only was proposed in [23, 24]. By complete rejection of currents from the input
signals, the fault-location algorithm free from CT errors has been obtained. Thus,
these algorithms appear to be completely immune to CT saturation, which is an
important advantage of them. On the other hand, the need for providing source
impedances from both line ends appears as a particular limitation of this algo-
rithm. This is so since a mismatch between the data provided and the actual source
impedances may happen and thus the fault-location accuracy can be degraded.
The algorithms from [23, 24] are formulated using a matrix description of the
transmission network.
In [186], several algorithms utilizing only the voltages, dispensing with current
transformers and thus eliminating the errors caused by saturation of current trans-
formers are presented. The algorithms are applicable to phase-to-ground faults,
phase-to-phase faults, and phase-to-phase-to-ground faults, thus not to three-phase
balanced faults. The algorithms utilize unsynchronized fault voltage measure-
ments from two ends of a line and do not require pre-fault data. Shunt capacitan-
ces of the line are fully considered, which is advantageous from the fault-location
accuracy point of view.
In turn, in [184] Liao introduced an interesting fault-location approach for sin-
gle-circuit lines utilizing only voltage measurements from one or two buses,
which may be distant from the faulted line. An advantage of the bus-impedance
matrix technique is utilized for that. With the addition of a fictitious bus where the
fault occurs, the transfer impedances of this bus and other buses are revealed as a
function of the fault location. It is shown in [184] that based on the relationship
between the bus-voltage change due to the fault and the transfer impedance, the
fault location can be derived. The shunt capacitance of the line is ignored first and
then fully considered based on a distributed-parameter line model.
A method for locating faults on two-terminal transmission lines based on the
fundamental components of fault and pre-fault voltage measured at the two ends
of a transmission line has been introduced in [341]. This methodology allows one
to establish a direct calculation procedure that is independent of fault and pre-fault
currents, fault type, fault resistance, synchronization condition of register devices
located on line ends, and pre-fault condition, either balanced or not. This is
achieved by defining a new concept called the ‘distance factor’(K ) in relation to

The fault-location algorithm from [341] is completely immune to CT satura-

7.4.2 Use of Two-end Voltages and One-end Current
It is well known from both experience and the literature [292] that if the CT satu-
ration occurs, it occurs at one line side only. Therefore, it seems to be advanta-
geous if the secondary currents of the CTs from the line side with no CT satura-
tion are included in the fault-locator input signals, besides the voltages acquired at
both line sides (utilized alone by the methods introduced in [23, 24, 184, 186,
341). As a result, still incomplete two-end signals are utilized, but more informa-
tion can be gained from the signals. The fault-location algorithm utilizing such in-
complete two-end signals measured asynchronously was introduced in [123, 271].
Let us derive the fault-location algorithm for the case with CT saturation occur-
ring at the line side B (Fig. 7.20). The other case: saturation of CTs at the side A
can be resolved analogously. The samples of three-phase currents and voltages
from the measurement units at both line ends (MU , MU ) are transferred via the
A B
communication channels to the fault locator. First, the currents from both line
ends are processed to recognize saturation. Algorithms known from the literature
[143, 144, 152] can be applied for this. As a result of identifying the CT saturation
at the line end B (in the considered case – Fig. 7.20), the three-phase current
measured at the side B: {i (n)}={i (n), i (n), i (n)} are further rejected, regard-
B Ba Bb Bc
less of how many CTs (only one, or two, or all three CTs) have become saturated.

7.4.3 Use of Two-end Currents and One-end Voltage
Modern microprocessor-based current differential relays exchange locally meas-
ured current phasors over long distances. For this purpose different forms of
communication means are utilized. The current differential protection principle
requires synchronization of digital measurements performed at different line ter-
minals. This is accomplished using the well-known global positioning system
(GPS) or other techniques (Sect. 4.3.3), [107].
This fault-location method is aimed at incorporating it into current differential
protective relays of the two-terminal power transmission or distribution line [119],
analogously as in [124] for a three-terminal line. It is assumed that such a fault lo-

7.4 Use of Incomplete Two-end Measurements 307
cator apart from three-phase currents from both ends of the line is additionally
provided with three-phase voltages from the local line terminal (Fig. 7.26). The
signals provided from both ends of the line are considered as synchronized. When
this is not so, the synchronization angle can be determined with use of the already-
known algorithms (Sect. 7.3.1).
Distinctive availability of the measurement signals for this method has been as-
sumed since the fault-location algorithm (being of an off-line regime nature) is de-
signed as the added feature for the current differential protection relay. The differ-
ential relay when applied to protect the two-terminal line utilizes phase currents
measured synchronously at both line terminals. Therefore, in order to incorporate
the fault-location function additionally to the protection function itself, the local
phase voltages (from the terminal A in further considerations) have to be supplied
to the relay. In this way, the differential relay, with the fault location added, can
identify the fault not only indicating whether it has occurred within the zone or
outside it (which is performed by the differential relay principle itself), but also
stating precisely at what distance from the particular line terminal it occurred.

7.4.4 Fault Location with Exchange of Limited Information
In [319, 320], a fault-location system for two-terminal, and for also multi-terminal
transmission lines, has been introduced. The algorithm used by this system is suit-
able for inclusion in a numerical protection relay, which communicates with re-
mote relay(s) and exchanges information over a protective relaying channel. The
data volume communicated between relays is sufficiently small to be easily
transmitted using a digital protection channel. The algorithm does not require data
alignment, pre-fault load-flow information, phase-selection information, and does
not perform iterations to calculate the distance to the fault. Pre-fault load flow, ze-
ro-sequence mutual coupling, fault resistance, power system non-homogeneity,
and current infeed from other line terminals or tapped loads do not affect the fault-
location accuracy.
In relation to Fig. 7.27, one can write down the formula, which comes from
comparison of the negative-sequence voltage at the fault point F, viewed from
both line terminals A, B, respectively:

7.5 Two-end Fault Location on Series-compensated Lines
7.5.1 Introduction
In Sect. 6.14 the one-end fault-location algorithms for both the single- and double-
circuit series-compensated transmission lines were presented in detail. Those algo-
rithms require representing the compensating bank (banks) in the form of the fun-
damental-frequency equivalent or by the estimated voltage drop across the bank.
This can be considered as a certain limitation of the one-end algorithms. With the
aim of overcoming such limitation, use of two-end measurements to series-
compensated line fault location has been proposed in [273, 340]. As a result, rep-
resenting the compensating bank is avoided, under the condition that only one
compensating bank is installed in the line. Such algorithms suit the application to
transmission lines compensated with fixed series capacitors (FSC) or thyristor-
controlled series capacitors (TCSC).

7.6 Recent Developments of Two-end Fault Location
When considering the solution of a problem with a particular number of un-
knowns it is important to determine how many equations can be formulated. If the
number of equations is smaller, then obtaining the solution requires making cer-
tain simplifying assumptions. In the case of the same number of equations as the
number of unknowns, the means to their solution is of interest. There is also a pos-
sibility for the case with redundancy, i.e., when it is possible to formulate more
equations than the number of unknowns. Such a case occurs if two-end synchro-
nized or unsynchronized measurements are utilized for fault location. The result-
ing redundancy can be utilized to obtain certain improvements in fault location.
This is observed in recent developments in this subject, as for example presented
in [187–189, 255].
In [187, 188], the fault-location technique not requiring line parameters, ob-
tained by utilizing the redundancy of information brought by the fault-locator in-

318 7 Two-end and Multi-end Fault-location Algorithms
put signals, has been delivered. In reality, values of line parameters may not al-
ways be available, and such an algorithm appears highly desired.
An optimal estimate of transmission-line fault location considering measure-
ment errors utilizing the redundancy has been proposed in [189]. It has been
shown that it is feasible to design an approach for detecting, identifying and re-
moving the possible bad measurements. In turn, when synchronized measurements
are utilized, possible synchronizing errors can also be detected. As a result of us-
ing this approach, improvement of the fault-location estimation accuracy can be
achieved.
A new accurate algorithm for locating faults on power transmission lines with
use of the two-end unsynchronized measurements of voltages and currents has
been presented in [255]. Simultaneous usage of two kinds of symmetrical compo-
nents, has allowed utilization of the redundancy with respect to the fault-location
equations. As a result, the synchronization operator is determined by applying
simple non-iterative calculations, even the distributed-parameter line model is
considered. This appears as very attractive from the practical point of view, since
it can be easily implemented into contemporary microprocessor-based protective
relays. Moreover, simple, but at the same time quite accurate determination of the
synchronization angle has been obtained when using the lumped-line model. This
angle was utilized for selecting the valid solution for the angle determined with
use of the distributed-parameter line model. However, apart from that purpose, it
can be considered also for simple checking of the synchronism of the distributed
measurements. Such checking appears to be attractive for differential protective
relay applications. Also, potential synchronization errors due to synchronizing de-
vice failures, such as communication problems or loss of the signal from the GPS,
could be easily detected.
7.7 Fault Location on Three-terminal Lines
Different availability of the fault-locator input signals can be considered in rela-
tion to application to three-terminal lines.
In Sect. 7.7.1 use of complete three-terminal measurements is considered, fo-
cusing on utilizing the unsynchronized measurements. Then, application of in-
complete measurements is taken into account. In particular, association of the fault
locator with current differential relays is proposed in Sect. 7.7.2. Then, use of
measurements acquired at only two line ends is considered and optimized. Finally,
the problem of defining the minimal measurements to provide for the fault-locator
input signals is addressed.
Apart from presenting the procedures for calculating the distance to fault, the
selection algorithms, aimed at finding which section of the line is faulted, are also
considered here. In order to achieve high accuracy of fault location, the distrib-
uted-parameter line model (the line sections are drawn with a thick line and not
with use of the rectangle as an impedance symbol) will be utilized.

320 7 Two-end and Multi-end Fault-location Algorithms
The fault may occur at any of the three line sections (faults: FA, FB or FC in
Figs. 7.33 and 7.34). The distance to the particular fault, measured from the par-
ticular bus (A, B or C) up to the fault point is denoted by d , d , d , respectively.
A B C
So, there are three hypotheses regarding placement of the fault in a particular line
section: A–T, T–B or T–C. In general, one can distinguish the following ap-
proaches:
• all three hypotheses regarding indication of the faulted-line section are consid-
ered and after calculating the distances to fault (d , d , d ) with use of three
A B C
subroutines, the judgment on selecting only one solution (the valid solution),
which corresponds to the actual fault position, is performed;
• first, the faulted-line section is identified and then the distance to fault for this
section is determined.
In [80], a fault-location method for two- and three-terminal lines has been pre-
sented. As the input signals of the fault locator, complete two- and three-terminal
measurements, both synchronized and unsynchronized, have been considered.
Three-phase voltage and current phasors from the line terminals are processed for
determining the distance to fault (d) and the synchronization angle (δ) if unsyn-
chronized measurements are considered. So, there is one unknown (d) and two
unknowns (d and δ) in the case of synchronized and unsynchronized measure-
ments, respectively. However, on using complete three-phase voltage and current
measurement at all line terminals, a redundancy of the fault-location equations is
assured. For example, in the case of two-terminal line and synchronized measure-
ments, the distance to fault is calculated applying the least-squares estimates from
three complex equations or six real-number equations in one unknown, d. Simi-
larly, the redundancy of the fault-location equations is assured for fault location on
a three-terminal line.
In the fault-location method from [80], the line sections are represented with
the line series impedance matrix only. Thus, the line capacitances are neglected,
which could affect the calculation of the fault location. However, the authors of
this method state that the fault-location error is minimized due to the redundancy
of the fault-location equations, which leads to a squares estimate of the fault loca-
tion. Important advantages of the fault-location algorithm rely on the fact that it is
independent of fault type, insensitive to fault resistance, and does not require any
information on source impedance. Neither does it assume transposition.
Another important contribution to fault location on three-terminal lines is pre-
sented in [4]. The technique described in [4] makes use of incremental, modal
components (the phase values are transformed into three modes: an earth mode
and two aerial modes) of voltages and currents rather than total, phase values, as it
was for the method presented in [80]. The contribution in [4] is based on the ap-
proach of the fault-location method developed earlier for a two-terminal line
[135]. Thus, the distributed-parameter line model is fully utilized and the fault lo-
cation in (7.8), developed for a two-terminal line is applied.
The fault-location algorithm [4] is designed for both synchronized and unsyn-
chronized three-end measurement of voltage and current. In the case of unsyn-

7.7 Fault Location on Three-terminal Lines 321
chronized measurement, the shifting of the data at the unsynchronized end(s) is
considered. For this purpose, the voltage at the tee point (T), based on the knowl-
edge of the pre-fault power frequency voltage and current phasors at all the line
terminals is determined, applying the distributed-parameter models of all line sec-
tions.
It is important to identify the faulted leg of the tee (the faulted-line section) be-
fore determining the distance to fault [4]. The technique consists in evaluating the
voltages at the tee point based on the knowledge of the fault current and voltage
phasors at the three ends. With reference to Fig. 7.33, one can state that the fault is
in the section A–T if the voltage at the T point transferred analytically from the
buses B and C (superscript: B and C):

7.7 Fault Location on Three-terminal Lines 325
Three fault estimates are calculated assuming the fault to be on the A–T, T–B
or T–C segment of the line, respectively.
A selection procedure is required to indicate the faulted-line segment, i.e.,
which of the subroutines (SUB_A, SUB_B or SUB_C) is valid, i.e., corresponds
to the real fault. In the first step of the selection procedure, the results of the fault
distance and resistance calculations are utilized. The subroutine that yields the dis-
tance to fault indicating the fault as occurring outside the section range (outside
the range: from 0 to 1.0 p.u.) or/and the calculated fault resistance of negative val-
ue, has to be surely rejected.
The second step of the selection is used when the first step is not sufficient. In
the second step, the remote source impedances (behind the terminals B and C – if
it is considered that the fault locator is installed at the station A (Fig. 7.35)), are
calculated for different subroutines [124]. Having calculated the impedances of
the sources behind the remote buses B, C – in relation to both subroutines
(SUB_B, SUB_C), first it is checked in which quadrant of the complex plane they
are placed. The actual equivalent source impedance is of the form of an RL
branch, i.e., is considered as placed in the I quadrant of the complex impedance
plane. If the calculated source impedance lies outside the I quadrant, then this sub-
routine is false and has to be rejected. Otherwise, if at least two subroutines (out of
three) still remain, then the selection has to be continued. The particular subrou-
tine can be rejected also if the calculated value of the remote source differs from
the actual impedance. For this rare fault case a certain knowledge of the actual
equivalent sources behind the line terminals is necessary. This is not a serious li-
mitation since for the other fault-location algorithms that utilize incomplete three-
end measurements [23, 117, 192, 213], the impedances of the sources are involved
even in calculation of the distance to fault.
7.7.3 Use of Two-end Measurements
The demand and importance of developing fault locators for three-terminal lines
under the availability of two-end synchronized measurements of voltages and cur-
rents (Fig. 7.38) has been introduced and justified in [192]. This is of practical im-
portance since the measurement infrastructure of the tapped line is usually rather
poor, or there are no communication channels for sending measurements from the
end of the tapped line.
It is considered in the fault-location methods presented in [115] and [192] that
phasor measurement units from two line ends (PMU , PMU ) provide the fault
A B
locator (FL) with three-phase phasors of voltage and current (U , I , U , I )
A A B B
measured synchronously (Fig. 7.38). Fault location is based on using three subrou-
tines, designed for locating particular faults (FA, FB, FC) and selecting the valid
subroutine.
Comparison of the voltage at the tee point T, obtained by analytical transfer of
signals measured at the end A (according to (7.97)) and at the end B (according to

326      7 Two-end and Multi-end Fault-location Algorithms
(7.95)) allows preliminary selection of the faulted-line section. If these voltages
match each other, then there is a fault FC on the tapped line. Otherwise, there is a
fault FA or FB on the main route of the line (sections: A–T and T–B). Distin-
guishing between the fault FA and FB can be performed on the basis of the calcu-
lated distance to fault [115, 192].

7.7.4 Use of Minimal Measurements
In [117], the fault-location algorithm for three-terminal lines using the limited
measurements, as compared to the earlier known approaches, has been presented.
In particular, only the one-end measurements of three-phase current and voltage
are utilized as the fault-locator input signals (Fig. 7.41). Additionally, information
on amplitudes of pre-fault currents, i.e., amplitudes of pre-fault positive-sequence
currents under the assumption of complete symmetry, from the remaining sections
of the line has to be provided as the input data. Moreover, detailed impedance data
of the network (for both the line sections and equivalent sources behind the line termi-
nals) has to be provided as the fault-locator input data. The method is based on the
symmetrical-components approach applied for formulating all three subroutines
designed for locating faults on the respective line sections.
The final step in the fault-location algorithm relies on selecting a valid subrou-
tine, i.e., on indicating which of the subroutines yields results consistent with the
actual distance to fault and fault resistance. The subroutine that yields distance to
fault outside its line section, and/or negative fault resistance, is surely false and
has to be rejected. If it is not so, other criteria have to be utilized. In the study car-
ried out the following criteria quantities were utilized:

7.8 Fault Location on Multi-terminal and Tapped Lines 329
• total fault currents in faulted phases (ought to correspond to the measured cur-
rents);
• amplitudes of the total fault current in healthy phases (ought to be close to ze-
ro); and
• boundary conditions for faults involving earth.

7.8 Fault Location on Multi-terminal and Tapped Lines
In Chap. 2, the basic models of multi-terminal and tapped lines are introduced.
The networks presented there are limited to the three-terminal line case (Figs. 2.7
and 2.8) and the network with one tapped line (Fig. 2.9). However, in real power
networks one can find lines with numbers of terminals higher than three and also
lines with more than one tap for feeding the load. Use of the fault-location algo-
rithms, which were presented in Sect. 7.7, is limited to a three-terminal line or to a
line with a single tap. Therefore, those algorithms require certain modifications be-
fore being applied to multi-terminal lines.
In Fig. 7.42, a scheme of the multi-terminal line is shown. It has four terminals
with power generation, and thus not less than three, as required in the definition of
multi-terminal lines introduced in [350]. In the case of five terminals there are
three tap points (T1, T2, T3) to which the tapped lines (T1–C, T3–E) are con-
nected with the sources of power generation, and the tapped line (T2-D) feeding
the load. Distributed generation included into distributed systems changes the
power flow, normally radial in distribution systems, to a multi-directional one
[81]. For the five-terminal lines there are four hypothetical locations of faults on
the main route of the line (A–T1–T2–T3–B) and three hypothetical locations on
the tapped lines (T1–C, T2–D, T3–E).

330 7 Two-end and Multi-end Fault-location Algorithms

Figure 7.43 shows an example of the tapped line with a source of generation at
the bus A and alternatively also at the bus B [3]. Thus, generation is at two of the
terminals, which is in compliance with the definition of the tapped line introduced
in [81]. There are also four tapped lines feeding the loads, which are usually bal-

systems [33].

A variety of algorithms for locating faults on multi-terminal and tapped lines
have been developed so far. For example, fault location on a multi-terminal line
has been reported in [218]. This method uses magnitudes of differential current at
all terminals for locating faults on multi-terminal two parallel lines. The method is
based on a three-terminal fault-location algorithm and an equivalent conversion
from the n-terminal to the three-terminal system is applied.
In [1] use of synchronized three-phase voltages and currents at all terminals for
fault location is considered. The algorithm using voltage differentials at terminals
to gradually reduce a multi-terminal line into a two-terminal line containing the
faulted section is applied there. Then, a reactive power-based method is used to
locate the fault.

7.8 Fault Location on Multi-terminal and Tapped Lines 331
An approach from [68] uses synchronized current inputs from all terminals and
uses two different methods to locate the fault on parallel double-circuit multi-
terminal transmission lines:
• impedance relay method (employs an impedance calculation); and
• current diversion ratio method.
In [310], an analysis and evaluation of multi-terminal fault location have been
presented. The technique proposed there uses the voltage from two terminals and
the current data from all terminals of the line. The measurements are considered as
performed synchronously with use of the GPS.
In [23] a fault-location method for a multi-terminal transmission line using
synchronized voltage measurements was introduced. It contains a simple new pro-
cedure for identifying the faulted-line section first. Then, to exactly locate the
fault on this section, a method is described that uses the synchronized voltage
measurements at all terminals. The main advantage of this method [23] is that the
current-transformer errors in the current measurements can be avoided. The me-
thod assumes that the source impedances are available. The method readily lends
itself to untransposed lines and is free from the pre-fault conditions.
An interactive approach to fault location on distribution overhead lines with
load taps is presented in [3]. However, the approach can be applied to transmis-
sion networks as well. The cited paper presents a novel technique in single-ended
fault location for overhead systems based on the concept of incremental (pure
fault) components of voltages and currents rather than total quantities. The incre-
mental fault-path current at the assumed fault point is determined. In order to find
the actual fault point, the assumed fault position is shifted in an interactive fashion
in such a way as to obtain the minimum value of the fault-path currents from
healthy phases. It is shown that the fault locator is highly insensitive to variations
in source impedances (both the local and remote) and to the presence of taps with
variable loads.

8 Fault Location in Distribution Networks
Abstract The objective of this chapter is to review basic fault-location algorithms
used in distribution lines. First, it gives a review of the standard fault-location
technique, namely impedance-based methods used in distribution networks. Then
it gives a short review of the non-standard fault-location techniques, such as high-
frequency-related methods, traveling wave and wavelet transform, for distribution
systems.
8.1 Introduction
Fault location in distribution medium-voltage (MV) networks has been a subject
of interest to utility engineers and researchers [44, 79, 261]. Information on accu-
rate fault location available just after the fault helps utility personnel to expedite
service restoration and to make adequate reconfiguration of the network for reduc-
ing outage time and operating costs. Therefore, more efficient methods for fault
location, supply restoration and high-quality customer service, are highly required
[3, 263].
Fault location in distribution networks (DN) creates new problems compared
with the same task in HV and EHV transmission lines. In HV and EHV networks
each transmission line may be equipped with a dedicated fault locator (FL). In
such a case, the FL algorithm is a numerical procedure that converts voltage and
current, given in a digital form, into a single number being a distance to fault. In
contrast to the transmission lines, the distribution networks are usually non-
homogeneous, with branches and loads along the line, which make the fault loca-
tion difficult [79, 261].
Distribution systems, also called medium-voltage (MV) systems deliver the
electrical energy to final step-down transformers at a voltage below 132 kV (this
value may be different in particular systems). The MV networks provide suppliers
direct to large customers, but the vast majority of consumers are connected at low
voltage via distribution transformers (MV/LV) [73, 87, 327].
The scheme of a typical distribution system is presented in Fig. 2.33 (Chap. 2).
The MV networks are supplied from HV/MV transforming substations. The elec-
trical energy is then transported via a series of underground-cable and overhead-

334 8 Fault Location in Distribution Networks
line circuits to the customers. In some cases a dispersed generation (DG) can be
connected to the network. The particular line sections are of length from a few
hundred meters to some dozens of kilometres. The distribution voltages in a spe-
cific service territory are likely similar because it is easier and more cost effective
to stock spare parts when the system voltages are consistent. Although due to dif-
ferent loads and the network development, separate feeders are made up of sec-
tions with different technical data: varying cable cross-sections and OH line pa-
rameters. The configuration layout and complexity of distribution networks vary
widely depending on the application.
In DN networks, FLs are usually assumed to be of a centralized type, i.e., they
measure the quantities common for the whole substation (busbar voltages and
transformer currents), which makes accurate fault location more difficult. Four
fundamental factors contribute to this:
• If a current of a faulty line is not directly available to the FL, a certain error is
introduced when assuming the transformer current during a fault to be a current
of the faulty line; moreover, it is not possible to compensate accurately for the
pre-fault load current of the faulty line.
• MV lines may be multi-terminal and/or contain loops that creates well-known
problems for one-end fault location as, in general, there is no indication on a
single fault position (few alternatives appear as possible).
• In the case of a MV line, there are often loads located between the fault point
and the busbar; since the loads change and are unknown to the FL it is difficult
to compensate for them.
• MV lines are mainly cable feeders that creates additional problems with ade-
quate representation of the equivalent scheme, when compared with overhead
lines.
8.2 Faults in Distribution System
Practical fault-location methods based on the use of current and voltage phasors
have been implemented in the feeder-protection devices. The reliability and accu-
racy of substation-based fault locators is questionable because of numerous fac-
tors.
The factors that are mostly influenced by the type of neutral grounding are dis-
cussed in Sect. 2.5. The principle of DN neutral grounding must be considered
when a fault-location method is used. The way the neutral is connected to the
ground determines the behavior of a power system during a single phase-to-
ground fault. The phase-to-phase faults, practically, are not influenced by the used
method of the network neutral grounding. Some general related problems and used
techniques that can reduce errors will be discussed in the following sections [106].

8.2 Faults in Distribution System 335
8.2.1 Solidly Grounded Networks
The idea of impedance-based methods used for fault location in solidly grounded
DN is very similar to that applied for transmission lines. This type of DN net-
works are the most common in North America. The ungrounded network will re-
quire grounding transformers, which are distributed around the network, resulting
in fewer sources of ground current. The net effect of this and of the latter two
types of grounding is to reduce the magnitude of the ground current [14]. This can
be seen as an increase in zero-sequence source impedance. Techniques to locate
faults on these networks will not differ from those for solidly grounded networks
except for the reduced accuracy of the computational techniques.
The unique topography of solidly grounded distribution systems presents many
challenges for fault locators at the substation. These include:
1. Conductor sizes change, thus making impedance calculations non-linear. One
possible solution is to model the line and create a nomograph.
2. Multiple feeder taps and laterals.
3. Inaccurate models/system data and dynamic configurations can affect results.
4. Effects of fault impedance can be significant.
5. Less energy to establish clean arcs.
6. Evolving fault characteristics and magnitudes can fool a relay’s ability to se-
lect the correct fault type.
In the case of a phase-to-ground fault, the reactance algorithm using the zero-
sequence voltage and the zero-sequence current of the faulted feeder may be used
to compensate for the effect of the tapped loads with wye-delta distribution trans-
formers. Another approach is to use the capacitive current of the feeder (important
if a large portion of the feeder consists of cable). One can also improve the fault
location for ground faults by using the ground or residual current instead of the
faulted phase current.
Another method uses an on-line calculation of the source impedance (behind
the unit) and the load impedance to compensate for the tapped loads (in addition to
a complete compensation for the reactance effect – which is discussed in Chap. 6)
in a radial distribution network. The load impedance can be estimated using the
pre-fault data (Fig. 8.1):

Traditional Methodologies
Often, faults are located without the use of any measurements. Location is simply
made through physical indications, field methods, and brute force methods such
as:
• restoration through switching;
• restoration through recloser operation;
• indication through fuse and fault-locator operation;
• downed wires, customer calls, maps;
• relay targets;
• DC thumping of underground circuits; and
• smelling burnt cables.

8.2 Faults in Distribution System 337
Observant Technologies
The ability to collect data further improves upon the success of locating faults
through such techniques as:
• local detection with communications feedback;
• “fault was upstream or downstream”;
• intelligent metering with modem, cellular-based devices, LOCATE-type de-
vices;
• detectors sending feedback through SCADA;
• Satellite-based location or carrier packages.
• choice of passing on information to an “interpreter” (i.e., a person) or to an “in-
terpretive device” (i.e., a substation HMI or DMS); and
• fault recorders.
Intelligent Technologies
Due to complexity, intelligent technologies are being applied for distribution fault
location. These include:
• artificial intelligence, neural networks to “learn” system characteristics; and
• distributed intelligence in substations to pull together information for best
guess, confidence factors.
Although evolving, competition may arise among observant technologies dis-
persed throughout the system, but integrated together, and advanced intelligent
technologies. These are briefly discussed in Chap. 9.
8.2.2 Locating Faults on Compensated Distribution Networks
The FL in high-resistance ground faults networks is a very complicated task. At
present the fault location is determined by dividing the faulted feeder into sections
by a disconnector and closing the substation circuit breaker against the fault until
the faulty line section is found. This is time consuming, since the operation of dis-
connectors requires a patrol moving in the terrain [221]. The other indication and
location methods proposed in the literature, are based on the direct measurement
of the basic components of the currents and voltages, on analyzing their variations
or their harmonic components with different methods, or on mixed versions of
these methods. The difficulty with the accurate location of ground faults in high-
impedance grounded networks is that the fundamental-frequency fault currents are
often small compared to the load currents, even in the case of very low fault resis-
tances [95].
In the promising methods it is assumed that the zero-sequence currents and the
neutral to earth voltage are available as complex values, so the magnitude and the

338 8 Fault Location in Distribution Networks
phase angle of their fundamental signal must be calculated from the measured sig-
nals [221, 248]. The algorithms are based on determining the total phase-to-
ground admittance as seen from the substation and the unbalance of each feeder of
a HV/MV substation.
The determination of the phase-to-ground admittance (for zero-sequence
equivalent circuit) of the whole system makes it possible to calculate the ground
fault current much more accurately than by using rough tabular values of the
phase-to-ground susceptances from the network data base. The change in the un-
balance of the feeder is a sensitive indicator with highly resistive ground faults.
The unbalance factor k is a normalized complex parameter indicating the phase
and the magnitude of the asymmetry of the three phases to ground. Its value de-
pends on the topology and the nature of the system (overhead lines, underground
cables).
After the fault indication, the fault location can be determined by connecting
the faulted feeder into a closed ring with some healthy feeder usually by a remote-
controlled switching device. In a compensated network this can be made without
outage to customers. Details of the algorithm are presented in [221].
The calculation of the zero-sequence impedances can be sometimes inaccurate,
especially in the case of underground cables.
8.2.3 Locating Faults on Underground and Paralleled Cables
Underground Cables
Locating faults on underground transmission or distribution lines is difficult to
achieve using microprocessor relays. First, the zero-sequence impedance changes
due to the distributed shunt capacitance along the entire line/cable (Fig. 8.2). The
capacitance can change depending on the system voltage, stored charge, different
zero-sequence return paths, and other factors. The effect can be likened to infeed
from unpredictable sources along an entire transmission line.
Fig. 8.2 Distributed capacitance along under-
ground cable
Moreover, the ohmic value of the cable is usually small, so a minute error in the
impedance model results in large errors in predicting fault location.
In practice, utilities use some form of pre-location followed by one or more
methods to pinpoint the location of the cable fault. The methods used depend pri-
marily on voltage class (transmission or distribution) and installation (conduit or
direct burial). There are generally two categories of fault locating: terminal meth-

8.3 Review of the Standard Fault-location Techniques for Distribution Systems 339
ods and tracer methods. These methods of fault locating usually take place after a
fault has occurred and has been cleared by protective relaying.
Terminal methods measure electrical quantities at one or both ends of the cable
circuit. Terminal methods are usually used to “pre-locate” the fault. The most
popular terminal methods include “bridge” techniques, like the Murray-loop, and
radar/low- or high-voltage pulse methods [15].
Tracer methods are most useful for “pinpointing” the location of the fault, and
usually require walking the cable route in the field. The most popular tracer meth-
ods are acoustic (“thumper”) techniques and earth gradient (applying a source and
measuring return current) methods, although many other methods are used. Recent
developments in using the transient voltage and current waves during a fault have
improved pinpointing cable fault location on distribution circuits. The method
measures the time between transient peaks to compute a distance to fault [328].
Paralleled Cable Circuits
Frequently, two conductors in parallel are used instead of one larger conductor. In
the case of insulated cables, a cable failure is characterized as a line-to-ground
fault on only one of the conductors. The line impedance in this case is not a linear
function of the distance to the fault. In the case of a radial circuit supplied from
one side only, the impedance is related to the distance to the fault as
Z = f(d)=d(2−d) (8.4)
where: Z is the normalized impedance to the fault (= 1 at the end of the line); d is
the distance to the fault (= 1 at the end of the line), which represents a parabolic
relation.
In the usual case of sources at both ends of the line, the situation resembles a
three-terminal line.
8.3 Review of the Standard Fault-location Techniques for
Distribution Systems
In this section, reviews of selected standard fault-location techniques (phasor-
based algorithms) proposed for distribution systems are presented [265].
8.3.1 Method Based on Lumped-parameters Network Model
The method presented in ref. [223] is based on the idea of fault location applied
for short transmission lines [62, 174], with all loads, including tapped lines, repre-

340      8 Fault Location in Distribution Networks
sented by a lumped-parameter impedance model placed behind the fault. This way
of compensating for tapped loads is accurate as tapped load impedances are much
larger than the feeder impedance.
The method is based on calculating both source and load impedances based on
pre-fault and fault voltages and currents measured at the substation. The load im-
pedance is calculated as in (8.1) while the source impedance behind the fault loca-
tor is calculated as in (8.3).
To avoid inaccurate calculation of source impedance for a small difference be-
tween fault and pre-fault values, a negative-sequence network is used for unbal-

the apparent location of the fault are ignored and the loads on a lateral are
considered to be present at the node to which the lateral is connected.

Two more estimates of the distance are obtained by considering that the fault
