The described system of combined wavelet transform and artificial neural net-
work results in increasing quality and considerable decreasing time of fault loca-
tion in transmission line. Wavelet transform allows high precision in determining
the propagation times of traveling waves. In consequence, the accuracy of the fault
location is very high as well. On the other hand, use of ANN results in higher reli-
ability of the algorithm to fault location, because the system with ANN is much
more selective to traveling waves and much more resistant to disturbances that are
present in a power system. The time response of such a system is also very good
because it is only slightly longer than the time required to propagate waves from
fault point to relay.
Test results have demonstrated that this approach can be used for accurate de-
termination of the fault-inception time, fault-type classification and distance to

9.3 Application Examples 403
fault estimation. It is seen that more advanced use of WT in power-system auto-
mation needs application of additional tools for recognition and identification of
information delivered by this method. That’s why the WT method is frequently
joined with an another technique. For example, the good time-resolution feature of
WT may be connected with ANN or FNN (fuzzy neural network) techniques [35,
139, 241, 339]. The general scheme of the signal processing includes the follow-
ing steps:
1. Voltage and current signals conditioning; in this process a DC component in
the current waveform is removed.
2. Voltage and current signals wavelet decomposition: determination of details
(D) and approximations (A).
3. Rough estimation of fault place.
4. Application of FNN to accurate fault location.
Rejection of DC from the current waveform is needed because the WT is not
suitable for non-oscillation components. In step 2 it is assumed that a discrete WT
is applied, however CWT methods may also be considered [27]. The final result is
obtained from FNN application [139].
Fault Location in Distribution Networks
Traveling-wave methods for distribution network and cable fault location have a
long history [70, 71, 328, 346]. The justification for using such techniques is ex-
plained by the domination of high-frequency post-fault current and voltage tran-
sients, especially when ungrounded or compensated networks are considered. The
wavelet transform is employed to extract these transients and the transient charac-
teristics are used to implement fault location.
The straightforward application of such an algorithm is based on utilizing the
wavelet transformation with a complex-valued mother function [27, 98, 247]. In
the method reported in [95] the following mother wavelet is used:

9.3.5 Genetic Algorithms Application
The special difficulties of the fault location take place in the case of branching net-
works with non-homogeneous sections. Such a condition may be met in distribu-
tion as well as in transmission networks. The fault location based on the voltage
and current phasors yields more than one location that could not be properly se-
lected [348].
Different methods are proposed for resolving the selection problem. The gen-
eral approach is based on application of an algorithm for searching for some simi-
larity between the recorded post-fault voltage and current transients and stored
signals related to the known (previously recorded or simulated) faults. The stored
signal can be in the form of the recorded time-variable phasors or simply wave-
forms. The selection procedures are based on the fact that in the complex network
its response to a fault depends, among other things, on the place of fault. It is usu-
ally assumed that the type of fault can be determined before starting the selection
procedure. The general algorithm is thus composed of the following steps.
1. determine the type of fault;
2. estimate a distance to fault and set of possible fault places; and
3. select most likely result.
In the second step different methods can be used: differential-equation-based,
impedance-based, traveling-wave or some other algorithm. The selection proce-
dure decided on the effectiveness of the hole algorithm. In some of the proposed
methods both the second and third steps are connected, creating the main proce-
dure.
A promising selection procedure was formulated in the language of an optimi-
zation problem where the criterion function is related to matching the post-fault
recorded file with the stored set of process files. This problem is suitable for ge-
netic algorithms application as an optimization tool.
The most advanced algorithm of this type is presented in [162]. It is assumed
that in the analyzed network area there are defined numbers of digital fault record-
ers (DFRs) but only limited data are available (‘sparse data’). This is because
some of them may not be triggered during a fault or in some network nodes DFRs
may not be installed.
The authors utilize the phasors for matching. The matching degree can be rep-
resented by a value obtained from the following cost function.

The cost function f(d, R) has a non-negative value and will be zero when the
f
phasors obtained from the simulation studies exactly match those obtained from
the recorded waveforms. The best fault-location estimation is achieved when the
cost function is at a minimum. Therefore, the problem of fault-location estimation
is actually the optimization problem. Since there may be several local minimum
and maximum points, it is difficult to use the gradient-based method to find the
global minimum. In fact, this is a good problem for application of a GA. This re-
quires formulation of the fitness function (see Sect. 9.2.4), which in contrast to
(9.43) should take the maximum value for the best matching. The following fit-
ness function was proposed [162]:
g(d,R )=C − f(d,R ) (9.44)
f max f
where: C is the maximum value of f(d, R) in the current population.
max f
The algorithm is suitable for the situation in which the conventional algorithms
cannot be applied because some recorded data is not available. However, a system
model including the static parameters and topology is required.
The searching process is run according to the GA methodology: at the begin-
ning, the initial population is generated randomly. Then posing the fault according
to the initial population, the short-circuit study is carried out to obtain the simu-
lated during-fault phasors and further calculate the fitness value for each individ-
ual. The next generation is produced by applying the three steps as described
above. The process is repeated until the best match is found.
The similar problems with selection between a few results also arise in the case
of the fault location in distribution networks. They also can be formulated in the
category of optimization problem and resolved by using GA.
AI techniques are in the process of fast development and evolution. The practi-
cal experiences of using different structures of ANNs and fuzzy-reasoning meth-
ods in real faults have shown that they are applicable and worthy of consideration
in solving fault-location and protection problems. They can be even more effective
when assisted by modern optimization and signal processing methods.
